Hon. CHARLES FITZPATRICK (Minister of Justice) moved second reading of Bill (No. 51) respecting contracts for government works.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time and House went into committee thereon.
On section 1-tenders to be invited ; exceptions ; contracts to be awarded by the Governor in Council-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The first clause practically re-enacts the law as we have it now ; that is to say, it provides that the minister shall invite tenders for all works of which the estimated cost exceeds $5,000, the exceptions being those works which are of immediate and urgent necessity and those of which the estimated cost does not exceed $5,000. The new feature is the second paragraph, which provides that all contracts let by tender are to be let, not by the minister directly, but by the minister under the control and with the approval of the Governor in Council. Having looked into the law, I found it necessary to make this change. As a matter of fact, contracts for works costing less than $5,000 have been let without tender, but there has been no legislative sanction for that. I am making this change so as to provide for the full approval of council to every contract that is made.
As the laws stands, I understand that all contracts must be let by tender.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The law as contained in 31 Victoria, chapter 12, section 20, re-enacted in the Revised Statutes as chapter 36, section 13 provides that all contracts shall be let by tender except works of im-

mediate and urgent necessity ; but in 1880 an Order in Council was passed authorizing the letting of contracts without tender in which the amount involved did not exceed $5,000. When X became Minister of Justice, on looking into the matter, I found that there was no authority for such an Order in Council, and I thought it advisable to get statutory authority for the practice. The only change is in the second paragraph, which provides for the approval of the Governor in Council.

It is exactly as I understood. I understood that the law in the past, except so far as modified by Order in Council, was that all works should be let by tender. The Bill is to legalize what has been done, and it is a very proper provision, with regard to some departments at any rate, that all contracts should be submitted to the Governor in Council.
Mr* INGRAM. How will this affect public works which were started three or four years ago and on which large sums of money have been spent, not by contract but by day's labour?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Any works of that kind can be carried on.

In my constituency several thousand dollars have been spent by day's work on a harbour ; and I do not know whether the government intend to continue the work by day's work or by contract, or whether this Bill will affect that work.

I do not understand that this Bill will affect a work of that kind at all, because it applies only to works under contract. The fact is, the government can spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on public works by private arrangement, by simply doing the work by day's work. The law does not prevent them. It only limits the powers of the government when they decide to do work by contract.

I was under the impression that any public work costing over $5,000 had to be done by contract.
Bill reported.

Bill (No. 53) to amend the Act respecting the Department of Railways and Canals, (Mr. Emmerson) read the second time and the House went into committee.
On section 1,
1. Section 11 of the Act respecting the Department of Railways and Canals, being chapter 37 of the Revised Stautes, is repealed and the following is substituted therefor :-
11. The minister shall invite tenders, by public advertisement, for the execution of all works, except in cases of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest, or in cases in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department, or in cases where the estimated cost' of the work is less than $5,000, and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
2. Whenever, in the case of any work, tenders are required to be, or are, invited, the minister shall submit all tenders received therefor to the Governor in Council, and the contract for the work shall be awarded under the direction of the Governor in Council.
The terms are precisely those of the Bill which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice has just explained.
What are we to understand by the term ' the officers and servants of the department'? Would that cover any number of men the department might employ to do a certain work ?
That would be the officers of the department, the regular employees of the department.

What are officers or servants of the department ? If this clause gives the minister the privilege of employing any number of men he pleases to do any particular work, it does away with the Act altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These words are taken from the old Public Works Act, 31 Vic., and I really do not know the meaning put upon them by the different governments. Strictly and literally they would mean all those who are in the pay of the department.

It ought to be limited to officers and servants who are permanently in the employ of the government. For the purpose of building a dam you might utilize day labourers who are idle part of the season, and in some cases that would be more economical, but the wording is such that it will allow the minister to dispense with a contract in every case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As these words occur in the first Bill, for which I am responsible, and the third reading of which has been held over, I will inquire and see how far we can limit the terms of the Bill.
Your engineers are officers and servants of the department. They might hire 100 or 1,000 men to do a work. Does that term include such men as the engineers may employ ?

It would not do to confine it to the permanent officials. The main point of this is to meet cases of pressing emergencies. Take for instance the work on the Welland canal. We do not keep a permanent electrician there and consequently

we require to employ, from time to time, expert electricians to meet emergencies. If you were to limit us to the employment of permanent officials you would make it impossible for the department to secure the services of an expert who in cases where there was no permanent official, could be employed.
There is no limitation in the case of an emergency. You can employ then as many men as you like.
What is the change between the old law and the present ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It consists in this. Formerly when an appropriation was made by parliament, tenders were invited for the work, and the minister let the contract himself without going to Council at all. The intention of the amendment is merely to make it incumbent on the minister to go to Council with his contract so that it may receive the sanction of Council before it is finally awarded. I am not dealing with the question raised by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) as to the meaning of the words in my Bill, but, with the meaning of the words in the original law relating to works to be executed by the officers and servants of the department. My judgment would be that the words are somewhat elastic and I suggested a moment ago, in answer to my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) that the matter might be left over for consideration when the Bill is up for third reading. In the meantime, I might inquire what has been the practice in the past and what has been the construction put upon these words during the time the law has been in force, that is, since confederation. I think this is largely a question of usage and of the construction put upon the words by parliament, and we shall be able better to express it when it comes up for third reading.
In both Bills ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Tisdale) was not here when the Bills were introduced. There are three Bills. One has reference to contracts for government works. That stands in my name. It is a Bill of general application to be observed with respect to all government works. The next Bill is one to make the Act respecting railways conform with the General Act I have mentioned. I have amended the Act respecting railways and using practically the same terms as in the other. Then there is a Bill to make the Public Works Act conform with the General Act. The effect is the same in all-to compel the ministers to come to Council to get authority to let a contract.
Will the hon. miniate: read the clause in the old Act which was repealed-section 11 of chapter 37 of the '
Revised Statutes. We have not that before us.

Here is the clause :
The minister shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of all works, except in cases of pressing emergency-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That simply reproduces the other.
That was amended subsequently.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have the amendment here :
The minister shall invite tenders by public advertisement for the execution of all works, except in cases of pressing emergency, in which delay would be injurious to the public interest, or in cases in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department-
Then, the change comes in here :

or in cases where the estimated cost is
less than $5,000, and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders.
That was the amendment of 3 Edward VII, chapter 52.

Who will decide whether the matter is one of pressing emergency or not, or whether the work can or cannot be more economically executed by the officers and servants of the department, or, according to the third exception, whether it is or is not advisable to invite tenders.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The minister has been made the absolute judge since confederation. There has never been any change.
My hon. friend from South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has read section 11 of chapter 37, respecting the Department of Railways and Canals, and that is the one that, by this is repealed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
And, that at present is the law of the land ?
So far as railways and canals are concerned.
It is amended.

There is nothing cited here as amended, and chapter 37 of the Revised Statutes must be the legislation on that subject, so far as the Department of Railways and Canals is concerned. That section allows works to be done without tender for any of three causes. The first is where the estimated cost is less than $5,000, and it appears to the minister, in view of the nature of the work that it is not advisable to invite tenders. Now, am I right in that respect ? If so this seems to

me a change which it is not advisable to make. There is a multiplicity of small works in the Department of Railways and Canals. If an analysis were made of the work, carried on by this department, I believe that the works costing under $5,000 would be a very large proportion of the construction work done under that department. Any one conversant with the railway system knows how many of its new buildings and that sort of thing along the railway come within a cost of $5,000. This would allow the minister to do that sort of work as he pleases, without inviting tenders. And that will result in the work being given to interested persons. It will practically shut out any competition in all that class of work, and I do not think it is healthy or right to shut out that competition. If there is a station house to be built along the line of the Intercolonial, the mere fact that it will not cost more than $5,000 is no reason why we should not have healthy competition in the building of that station. And what is true with reference to such a station is true with reference to a very large class of works under the value of $5,000 in this department. Now, parliament adopts this amendment, and it will become the rule that all that class of work will go out without tender. What is the advantage of tender ? It is that you may curb unnecessary expense and secure competition, it is that money of the country should be expended as economically as possible. In the case of practically every one of these works there might be competition, and the effect of that competition would be to keep down the cost of construction. If there is any virtue in the tender system and in the economical administration of the public moneys, I think we ignore or deny that principle By this legislation. I am not in favour of extending this to the Department of Railways and Canals or the Department of Public Works. As to the other two cases, the first is ' except in cases of pressing emergency in which delay would be injurious to the public interest.' That, I think is all right and must be in the Bill. That is to prevent injury to the public interest in certain eases. As my hon. friend pointed out, this is absolute. Then there is the third case, ' in which, from the nature of the work, it can be more expeditiously and economically executed by the officers and servants of the department.'
That is in the decision of the minister, 1 suppose, as to whether' it can so be done. But as the clause stands, he cannot do it in the case of a $5,000 expenditure, and under the arrangements, unless he does it by his officers and servants. There would be no reason for putting that in as a second case at all unless it were contemplated that these officers and servants should be the officers and servants at the time* in pay of the department; otherwise it would all come in under the third case, the $5,000 expenditure, where it appears to the minister, in view of the nature or the work, that it is not advisable to invite tenders. Now, if the contention of the Minister of Railways is allowed that he can take one of his servants and make him superintendent of the job and employ help outside the employees of the department, why, that becomes as wide as it can become. I think it is dangerous and uneconomical.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I said some time ago, we are dealing with three different chapters of me Revised Statutes. We are dealing with the chapter which has reference to the control of government work, that was a Bill I had myself in my own name; then we are dealing with the chapter which has reference to the Public Works Act, and in addition to that, we are dealing with the chapter which has reference to government railways. That is the Bill we are now dealing with. Row, with respect to government works generally, provision was made that all public works should be let by tender, that was the original provision, with two exceptions: The first was with respect to works of an immediate and urgent necessity, and the next exception was in so far as the work was carried on by the servants of the department-I forget the exact words. Now, under the law as it stood an Order in Council was passed authorizing the minister to deal with a work in which the amount involved does not exceed $5,000 without inviting tenders. That Order in Council was passed in 1880 or 1881. Finding that there was no legislative authority for that Order in Council, 1 deemed it advisable to amend the law accordingly, and I did amend it some two sessions ago, but only with respect to public works, not with respect to the Department of Railways and Canals. Therefore, it is necessary now to amend the law with respect to tfie Department of Railways and Canals so as to make it conform with the Order in Council, and also with the general provisions applicable to the Public Works Act. The amendment was made with respect to the Public Works Act two years ago by 3 Edward VII., chapter 52, and the intention is to make that principle, which was then made applicable to the Public Works, now applicable to the Railways and Canals.
There is no limitation in case of emergency ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Then what seems to be necessary under that, would be to define the term ' servant and officers,' and that the minister will take into consideration before the third reading.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I thought I would inauire as to what the practice has been in

the past, not the practice of recent years, but since the Act has been in force, so as to find out how far we can make an amendment which will conform to the practice itself. '
I would rather see the Order in Council abolished.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It never had any
existence in law.
If I remember rightly, cases of emergency, by the rules and regulations, are decided by Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No, by the minister. My hon. friend has the experience of a min-inster in that department, whereas I have not, but I think he will find that the practice has been that the minister decided.

The aggregate amount of the increases is $22,316.25 and the aggregate amount of the decreases $6,160, leaving a balance of $16,156.25. I may say that most of these increases are in accordance with the law and the regulations of the department. The case of the inspectors, for instance, is determined by law. In regard to the deputy collectors, class A and first-class, excisemen, these increases are in accordance with the regulations which have been in existence for about fifteen years.
Is that increase of $16,156 an increase in salaries under the regulations and not due to an increase in the number of officers?

It is not due to an increase in the number of officers but last yen r we had what we call promotion examinations among the officers, and it is
' Mr. FITZPATRICK.
determined by the regulations that all who succeed in passing these promotion examinations receive promotion to the class to which they are entitled by the number of points they get in the examinations. The largest increase is $10,100 given to the first-class excisemen. These men were second or third-class excisemen, but having passed their promotion examination they are entitled under the regulations to the promotions which they received.

What is the system which the hon. minister at present carries out in reference to these widely distributed officers and the inspection of them in the performance of their duties? Have you here in Ottawa and throughout the Dominion a system of inspection to ensure that these officers are looked after in their work ?

We have inspectors in all the provinces. Take for example the province of Quebec; there are two inspectors to look after the head offices and the out offices. We have in Quebec five divisions. We have two inspectors to look after these five divisions. Each of these divisions has a collector who is the head of the division, but besides these officers we have also two inspectors, one for the Quebec district and another for the Montreal district. These two inspectors are obliged by the regulations and the law to go and inspect all the head offices and all the out offices in the province.
How often are these visits of inspection made?
Every three months.
For each district?
Yes, and once a month for every bonded warehouse.
To whom do these inspectors report?
To the department.
Do they make then- reports monthly?

Yes, after their visits. Besides that, I may add, we have four general inspectors, one inspector of distilleries, one inspector of bonded warehouses, one inspector of breweries and one inspector of tobacco factories.
Where are these four inspectors located?

These four are among the inspectors I have just mentioned. They have to look after the inspection of their own districts, but at the same time they have a general supervision over the whole country in their particular branches. Take the inspector of cigar and tobacco factories, for instance; he is living in the city of Montreal, he is attending to his duty there as inspector of the district, and at the same

time, once a year he is supposed to visit all the tobacco factories in the country.

He is supposed to; he does,
I suppose?
As a matter of fact he does.
And these inspectors report directly to the deputy of the hon. minister?
Yes.
What are the general conditions of the tobacco industry as it comes under the observation of the hon. minister's department as regards extension or growth?

The Canadian tobacco industry has increased largely of late years; in fact, about eight years ago there were only about 500,000 pounds of tobacco manufactured in this country, but now we have reached an output of nearly 5,000,000 pounds.
Do you mean manufactured out of Canadian product?

Yes. Some years ago when the law was changed, tobacco manufacturers * were permitted to mix foreign tobacco with Canadian tobacco to the extent of ten per cent, and in this 5,000,000 pounds are included that ten per cent.
How is it mixed-as a wrapper?

In cigar factories it is mostly used for wrappers' because the imported wrappers are more suitable than the tobacco which is grown in this country, but in the manufacture of cut tobacco they use also a quantity of foreign tobacco.
Personally what is the hon. minister's opinion from test as to the relative merits of foreign and home grown tobacco?

I may say that I am not a smoker myself. I remember that question was put to me last year by aD hon. member of this House and he was much surprised to hear me say that our Canadian tobacco was just as good as foreign tobacco. I was told so by men who had some experience in the matter although my opinion was controverted by some hon. members of this House whom I have the honour to see before me just now. I would not like to express as positive an opinion as I did last year but I am told by several competent men-I will not say that those who hold a contrary opinion are not competent-that we can grow in this country a very good tobacco which can take the place of foreign leaf.
Where is this growth chiefly extending?
The growth of tobacco is carried on especially in the counties of Essex and Kent, in Ontario and in Montcalm, Berthier, Joliette, L'Assomption and Rouville in Quebec.
These are practically the only sections of the Dominion in which tobacco culture is extensively carried on.

Practically. There is production also in the other counties, but
the tobacco raised in them is sold on the open markets and does not generally come into consumption through the manufacturers.
The minister still believes in radical' production for the Canadian tobacco industry.

I think that the protection that was given to the tobacco industry in 1896 has had a good effect, as has just been shown, because in 1896 a very small quantity of tobacco was grown or manufactured in this country. That production has now been multiplied ten times, and I suppose it will have a good effect.
Is any of the Canadian leaf tobacco exported ?

I do not think there is any large quantity, although some years ago an agent was sent, through the Department of Agriculture to Belgium to find if a market for our tobacco could not be opened there, but it did not result in success. I think our efforts should be to take hold of the Canadian market, and I think we can succeed in having our tobacco properly cured and properly prepared.

In the meantime you will compel the Canadians to consume their own
product as far as possible ?

Perhaps I may be responsible for some of the remarks that have been made by the minister with reference to the quality of Canadian as compared with foreign leaf. I do not desire to say one word reflecting upon the Canadian product, but I would be glad if the department with the technical knowledge they have would be able to so assist the manufacturers and producers that they would be able to assimilate the Canadian product in flavour and taste to the imported article. While the Canadian tobacco may be as good as any in the world still its flavour is sometimes repugnant to a smoker who is accustomed to using the imported tobacco. If an article is produced in Canada more like the American article, the consumption of the Canadian tobacco will be very materially increased and that of imported tobacco correspondingly reduced. I think that is the desire of the minister, I think that is what he is aiming at. It is an admirable policy and we want to encourage the home market for our produ-

cers, but we must produce an article in our own country that will, as nearly as possible, meet the wishes of the great number of smokers in this country. My own opinion is that that has not yet been accomplished, and as the quality of the leaf is equal to the foreign leaf the difficulty must be in the process of curing. When we can so cure our tobacco as to produce the flavour of the American tobacco we will find that the consumption of Canadian leaf in this country will be very much increased.

I quite agree with the hon. member for Haltou (Mr. Henderson). I myself come from the tobacco district. I do not know whether the minister uses tobacco himself or not, but if he does I shall be very glad to take him down there and give him samples of the very best tobacco, as I believe, that is grown in the world. We grow the quality of leaf there and I quite agree with the hon. member for Hal-ton that it is in the curing that we fall behind. I was speaking recently to a manufacturer of tobacco in my own town, an ardent supporter of the government, who told me that Canadian leaf, properly cured, is equal to any tobacco which is imported.
Hear, hear.

It is an industry which is growing very rapidly, and I must give the present government credit for fostering that industry to some extent. I believe that a great deal could be done to assist tobacco growing in our country. I know that we grow it there and our farmers have found it a profitable crop at present prices. I believe the industry should be assisted and that the farmers should be encouraged in the growing of tobacco. Under these conditions our people would be able to supply the largest part of the tobacco consumed in this country. I would ask the minister to make every effort to assist us in that distinct in encouraging the trade. I might also say to the hon. minister that I agree with the hon. member for Halton and that the advice I have from manufacturers there is that a great deal could be done to Improve the curing of Canadian leaf. I believe that the fault with our tobacco, at the present time, lies there.

I am very glad of the expressions of opinion which I have just heard from the hon. members. Since I have been at the head of the department I have taken a great interest in the question of tobacco growing and of fostering, as much as possible, the increased production and consumption of Canadian tobacco. I do not know why we should not succeed in having in this country Canadian tobacco consumed instead of foreign leaf tobacco.
I think that we can produce in this country just as good an article as the imported tobacco. Perhaps we cannot, in some instances, produce a leaf just as nice as those imported from Sumatra or Havana ; but Mr. HENDERSON.
there is no reason why good plug smoking and chewing tobacco should not be made entirely from Canadian leaf. It has been suggested that the curing of the tobacco in Canada has not been very good. Our producers have not perhaps been very successful in that respect ; but the government has taken every possible means to encourage them to give us a first-class leaf. A few months ago we sent to the state of Wisconsin, which has a similar climate to ours, some persons to study this question with reference to how the seeding is done and how the tobacco is cured. The governor of the state was good enough to place at the disposal of our agents his extensive farm, and to show them the various processes. They have reported to the Department of Agriculture, to which the question pertains more than it does to mine; but, at the same time, I am taking an active interest in the question, I feel strongly upon it, and I am going to do my best, and the government is going to do its best, to foster this industry in Canada. We found that the seeds used in Canada were not the best, and the two agents who visited Wisconsin are now delivering lectures in some parts of the country, and are supplying better seeds to the farmers. My opinion is that we should make extensive experiments on the experimental farm here. The Minister of Agriculture has already done something in that respect. I think we should try various kinds of seeds. I am glad to see that the feeling of this House is in favour of extending the production of Canadian leaf, and hon. members may rest assured that nothing shall be spared on my part, or on the part of the goverment, to encourage that industry, which is a very important one and deserves all the protection possible. We have been asked on several occasions by my hon. friend the Speaker and by other members to establish experimental farms in the districts where tobacco is produced on a large scale. We are considering that question, and if we find a means of making experiments on the experimental farm, we may afterwards establish experimental stations in some of the tobacco-growing districts.

I want to congratulate the minister on the efforts he is making on behalf of our tobacco growers. As an illustration, I may mention that only a short time ago I asked a tobacco manufacturer in my city if there was any prospect of our Canadian leaf being manufactured into cigars, and he told me that he had made some cigars from tobacco which had been cured for about four years, and had given some of them to some expert American cigar, men who had been over here, and they pronounced them the best cigars they had ever smoked. Therefore, it seems to me that there is no reason why our Canadian tobacco could not be manufactured into oigars.

I have not much confidence in the production of tobacco at the experimental farm at Ottawa. I think the minister will find it to be an absolute failure owing to the frost. The experiments should be carried on in a climate not so susceptible to early frosts. The production of tobacco in this country is not the difficulty. The counties of Essex and Kent alone, along with the counties in Quebec which the hon. minister has named, would produce far more tobacco than would be consumed in this country. The difficulty is that the flavour of the Canadian tobacco is not what the great bulk of the people of this country want. Whether it is better than or not as good as that of American tobacco, X will not undertake to say; but if you are going to obtain a large consumption of Canadian tobacco for ordinary smoking purposes, you must secure a flavour like that of the American leaf. For instance, If you can get a flavour similar to that of the tobacco manufactured by Sir William Macdonald in which I understand there is no Canadian leaf, there is no reason why you cannot supplant the American leaf ; and I am sure that could be done. There ought to be scientific knowledge enough in this country to discover where the defect is and to bring about the desired result. When you do that, people will buy the Canadian tobacco, not knowing whether it is Canadian or American, and you will have a very large consumption of our native tobacco. The production will take care of itself. Although there is only a limited area in the counties of Essex and Kent devoted to tobacco growing, that area produces an enormous crop. It makes a man think well of his country to pass through those counties and see the immense tobacco crop in those small fields ; and the production is capable of any degree of expansion. But let me impress this upon the minister, that he must exert himself to assist the curers of tobacco to obtain a flavour similar to that of American tobacco ; then I am satisfied that the consumption will go on as rapidly as we desire.

I do not wish to express my own personal opinion as to the superiority of the Canadian leaf or of the foreign leaf ; but I have been told by many competent persons that the supposed inferiority of Canadian tobacco is a mere matter of prejudice. I have known several persons who, after having smoked for years tobacco made by Macdonald, which is made entirely from foreign leaf, afterwards tried Canadian tobacco made by some other Canadian company, and declared it to be just as good as the other. I think it is more a matter of prejudice than anything else, and I hope that every one who smokes will try our good Canadian tobacco, and that the farmers will do their best to put on the market a first-class article.

The minister may be right; it may be largely a question of taste.
I am not saying that the Canadian tobacco is not as good as the American. It may be ; but that taste exists, and if we are going to have a large sale of Canadian tobacco, we must cater to the taste of the larger number. A very large number of smokers in this country prefer the flavour of tobacco made from the American leaf, and the efforts of the hon. minister should be along the line of assimilating the taste of the Canadian leaf to that of the American leaf. The moment that is accomplished, he will secure for Canadian tobacco a monopoly of the sale in this country.

Some seeding has been done on the experimental farm and some small experiments made with some success, but I do not think that the frost is prejudicial in this section to the growth of Canadian tobacco. Take the county of Montcalm, which is in the same latitude as Ottawa, there very good Canadian tobacco is grown, just ns good as that produced in the south. The state of Wisconsin is in the same latitude as Ottawa, why, therefore should we not produce in this section as good tobacco as is grown in Wisconsin ? The industry is in its infancy, but it is the duty of the government to protect that industry as far as possible and do everything possible to stimulate it.

The area in which you can grow tobacco in Canada is not at all limited. I saw tobacco grown forty years ago in districts where the frost was a great deal worse than it is to-day, and where you could not then grow wheat. There is no doubt a great deal of truth in the explanation of the hon. minister that the foreign leaf is preferred to the Canadian, simply because the people have acquired a taste for it. Let them begin to smoke Canadian leaf and they will find it just as palatable as the tobacco made by Sir Wm. Macdonald, of Montreal. I remember twenty years ago an old smoker telling me that he had smoked the Canadian twist made by the French habitant for 50 years and it was the best tobacco you could get. There is a lot of talk about the French, he said, but as long as they can make good tobacco, may God prosper them. Tobacco has been grown up in the Georgian Bay district, to my personal knowledge, for forty years, and can be grown in almost any county in Canada. But what I rose more particularly to inquire about was whether the government had made any effort at the experimental farm to ascertain whether tobacco could not be successfully grown in the prairies of the west, just as it is in the western prairies of the United States.
I cannot say whether experiments have been made in the west, but I am inclined to think not. I shall be glad however to call attention to the suggestion which I think is a very good one.

I understand from the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) that if we could grow tobacco similar to that manufactured by Sir Win. Macdonald in Montreal, that would settle the question at once. Is there any Canadian grown used in that manufactured by Sir William ?
I think the proportion is live million pounds of Canadian tobacco against nine million of foreign leaf show the increasing popularity of our tobacco.
Does he use Canadian leaf ?

No, he might use Canadian leaf, but his license is only for foreign leaf. I have been told, however, that in some cases those who have licenses for foreign leaf use the Canadian leaf. They pay the same duty as on the foreign leaf, 25 cents per pound, and mis up the Canadian leaf with the foreign, but I do not think Sir Wm. Macdonald uses any foreign leaf.

Representing, as I do, a constituency in which tobacco is very largely grown, I wish to express my appreciation of the fostering influence which the policy of this government has had on that industry. In South Essex the growth of tobacco was begun earlier than in any other county of Ontario. Before the birth of any hon. gentleman in this House, the French Canadians there grew their own tobacco, and have been smoking it with a great deal of pleasure ever since. It is not many years ago when they could only get 4 cents a pound for their tobacco and then could only sell it with difficulty, but during the past year, under present conditions, they have sold at least 3,000.000 pounds and realized some $300,000 when they could not realize much from other crops on account of the wetness of the season. The people will commend the government if the government will not only continue the present policy of protecting the Canadian leaf but also establish some experimental station in South Essex in order that the leaf may be perfected so as to suit the taste of even the most particular. In Kingsville, cigars are now being manufactured wholly of Canadian leaf and a most successful trade is expected to be developed in that line.' I would urge the government to continue the work of perfecting and protecting the Canadian leaf in every way possible.

I understood the hon. minister to say that all these different points wore inspected at least once a year. If he will turn to K-51, he will find that the Auditor General complains that the inspectors have not furnished certain information, and that Montreal had not been inspected since April, 1900. In his letter to the department of March 21, 1903, he complains that the city of Montreal has not been in-Mr. BRODEUR.
spected since 1900, and no explanation is given.
This is a matter which is brought to my attention for the first time and I shall inquire into it. The regulations provide for an inspection at least once a year.

The peculiar point about this is the remarkable fact that there has been no reply by the department to the Auditor General's letter.
Excise-to provide for duty pay to officers serving longer hours at other than special survey, $1,000.
The amount is small; to whom does it go?

This is to pay deserving officers engaged in special service on account of the long hours, and, in some cases the disagreeable character of their work. In some cases they serve from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m., being required to be present from the time the factory opens until it closes in the evening.
Among how many officers is that divided?

About twenty. Last year we spent about $700 on this account.
Excise-preventive service, $13,000.
What do the officers do for this service besides drawing their salaries?

The preventive service, as my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) knows is to prevent violation of the laws and to effect seizures where violations have taken place. These officers move about the country, and, wherever they find violations to have taken place, they make seizures. I am informed that last year, about sixty seizures were made. The presence of those officers in the community has a good effect and is itself a prevention of violation of the law.
Does the fewness of the seizures prove that violations are few, or does it mean that the officers do not discover them.
I think the violations are very few. We have first-class men connected with this service, some of whom have been with the department for many years. They are deserving men and are doing their best.
Do these preventive officers get any part of the proceeds of a fine?
Yes, I think the seizing officer, if he is a preventive officer, is given one-half the proceeds of the seizure.

I notice that the payments made last year to informers represent a small total and were paid to but few persons. The total amo'Tt paid was $838,

so that the total value of the seizures would be only about $1,600.
The penalties imposed by the judge usually are not large. They run from $5 to $100.
If a penalty is imposed and yet nothing can be collected, does the informer get anything?
We pay, in that case, one-quarter of the amount.
The idea being what ?

It has been the custom in the department for many years. And it tends to encourage the giving of the information.
Excise-travelling expenses, rent, fuel, stationery, &c., $62,000.
How does the minister regulate the travelling expenses of the officers?

In some cases officers must go to new places to remain for some time. If a bonded factory or brewery is started in a new place, we cannot choose a local man as officer, one who has not had experience. We have to send an officer from the department to look after the new establishment for a certain time. In that case, we pay not only travelling expenses but board.
How are the travelling expenses arranged?
They are paid what they actually spend in travelling.
For which they have to give vouchers?
Yes, as in the other departments.
How does the minister account for the increase in this estimate over last year?

We have to open new offices almost every mouth. New breweries, bonded factories and bonded warehouses are opened, and these have to be provided for. In fact, the expense is larger on account of the increase of population and consequently in the work.
Excise-to pay collectors of customs allowance for duty collected by them for 1904-5, $5,508.
What does that mean ?

In some places, where we do not wish to appoint a regular officer of the department, we obtain the services of the customs collector, to whom we pay 5 per cent on collections up to $3,000, over $3,000 and up to $5,000, $100 per annum ; over $5,000 and up to $10,000, $200 per annum; and over $10,000,	$250 per annum.
There is less expense than in the appointment of a regular officer.
Does the minister do that in every ease where it can be reasonably done?

In most of the cases where we can find a suitable officer in the Department of Customs, we generally make use of his services.
Excise-L. A. Frechette, for special translation, $100.
What is the special translation ?

We have special regulations and departmental reports to be translated. Take, for example, the bulletins of the department. These call for special knowledge on the part of the translator, because of the many technical expressions used. Therefore, we secure the assistance of Mr. Frechette who is the chief translator of the House of Commons. The documents to which I refer are not tabled in this House, so we cannot get them translated by the regular officers of the House. They are simply departmental documents.
Provisional allowance of not more than $100 each to officers in British Columbia, Manitoba1 and the Northwest Territories, whose salaries from any government source do not exceed $1,000, $1,500.

The reason for this vote is that we cannot get, in the provinces named, officers of the same class that we can get in the eastern provinces and for the same pay. As an instance, I may mention that I asked an hon. member of this House to recommend somebody for an office in British Columbia, and the party recommended absolutely refused to take the position at $506, which was the sum at which he would have to enter upon his work. Some years ago provision was made that all officers having a salary of $800 should receive $100 additional, and now we find it necessary to make this additional provision.
To enable the department to supply methylated spirits to manufacturers, the cost of which will be recouped by the manufacturers to whom1 it is supplied, and to pay for rent, light, power, freight, salaries, &c., $60,000.

This sum is to enable the department to purchase alcohol and wood naphtha for the manufacture of methylated spirits to supply manufacturers, and to pay for rent, light, power, freight, salaries, &e. The amount expended the last fiscal year was $50,645.06, and $26,466.91 for the last six months, expiring on the 1st of January last. The manufacture of methylated spirits was taken over from the bonded manufacturers and carried on by the department, as a protection to the revenue, July 1, 1888. It was known that these methylated spirits were being used as a substitute for genuine potable spirits, which was objectionable, not only from a

revenue standpoint, but as well on the grounds of injury to tbe public health. The duty was only 15 per cent per proof gallon as against the then duty of $1.30, and the existing duty of $1.90 on spirits. It was thus deemed necessary to take sole control of its manufacture and to supply It to responsible persons for stated purposes. Two grades were established, viz.: No. 1, consisting of about 25 per cent of wood naphtha, and No. 2, consisting of about 50 per cent. Grade No. 1 is supplied to varnish and other manufacturers who have obtained the necessary permit from the department, and who have entered into bonds, with sureties in the sum of $2,000, that such spirits shall only be used for the purposes mentioned, and in the premises described in their application. The present price of this grade is $1.10 per gallon.
How do you fix that price 7

We take about 15 per cent profit. If we use 75 per cent of wood alcohol for which we pay $1.40 and 25 per cent of grain alcohol, for which we pay about 25 cents, we add about 15 per cent to the cost of the raw material. As I say, the present price of this grade is $1.10 per gallon. It is used for the manufacture of varnish, liquid glue, mucilage, inks, leather dressings, stove and shoe polish, soap, &c. Grade No. 2 is supplied to the trade for burning, &c., without the issue of a permit, and without entering into bonds. This is due to the fact that the percentage of wood naphtha is so large that its use for potable purposes would be impossible. The reason of the price of the latter being higher than the better grade is owing to the large quantity of wood naphtha used, which costs the department $1.40 as against 25 cents per gallon paid for alcohol. East year we bought $43,332.55 worth, and we sold for $68,325.69.
Where did you get your raw material ?
We used to buy it from the Standard Chemical Company.
Where are their works ?
They have works at Cookshire, Fenelon Falls, and I think Toronto.
Are these all the places in which they manufacture ?
Those are the only places that I remember. I think they have four or five places.
How do you buy ?

A contract was made some years ago with the Standard Chemical Company when the system was introduced here. The first contract was made with the Rathbun Company, and they refused to carry it out, and we gave it to the Standard Mr. BRODEUR.
Chemical Company. I think that company is a combination of the Rathbun Company and the Standard Chemical Company, that is my impression. The contract ceased some years ago and was not renewed. After I entered the department I concluded it was not a very good system, and that it would be better to call for tenders, and we did call for tenders in the months of December and January. I am not quite sure, but I think the contract is to be awarded to some other firm.
What is the lowest tender 7

$1.29. The contract was given to the lowest tenderer with one exception

I must be frank with the House -there was a tender from an American firm offering to supply an American article free of duty ; but I refused to accept that tender, and recommended Council to accept the lowest tender for the Canadian article.
What did you pay before 7
$1.40, now we are getting it at $1.29.
What method did the hon. gentleman adopt in calling for tenders 7

We advertised in the newspapers for tenders for the supply of wood naphtha of a certain quality, which was to be approved by the department. We advertised in all the important papers of the country. The accountant informs me that he paid for advertisements in twenty-five papers.
Were any of those papers in Toronto 7

Yes, there was the ' News,' I am informed, and the Toronto ' Globe,' of course.
Salaries of officers, inspectors and assistant inspectors of weights and measures, $63,750.
Is there any report published by the department giving a detailed statement of the inspections made by the different inspectors of gas and electric plants 7
There is a report which will be found in Part II.
It is a very limited report merely giving the number of plants inspected.
It covers several pages of the report. I do not know whether my hon. friend has seen it or not but it is in the second part of the Inland Revenue Report.

I have not seen the one for this year but I have seen it in other years'. A number of municipalities throughout the

Dominion, in Ontario, at all events, are very much interested in what they call municipal ownership, and they ares very eager to secure information which the inspection of these various plants will give them. The only source from which they can get that information is through the government inspection.

The report, as far as gas inspection is concerned, is to be found at pages 22-52 of the Inland Revenue Report. There are thirty pages devoted to the inspection of gas.
' Mr. INGRAM. Is the method of reporting now adopted the same as it has been for years ?
Yes, the same system.
Is the inspection of weights and measures being carried on in the same basis as it was eight or ten years ago ?
No, there has been an improvement in respect to weights and measures.
What has been done ?

We thought a good way to deal with the question would be to have a chief inspector here. Some years ago we appointed a chief inspector who is looking after the work that is done by inspectors and assistant inspectors of weights and measures. He is looking after their accounts and at the same time wherever there is a complaint, he, being a practical man, goes and investigates the matter. I am doing my best to prevent a continuation of the deficit which has been met with for many years in that branch of the service.
What does it stand at now ?
Before I took charge of the department there was a deficit of $25,000 while last year there was a deficit of $18,000. I am strongly of the opinion that both ends should come together.
How are you going to make the two ends come together ?
I have asked the inspector to look into the accounts and report ways in which more economy can be observed. I feel certain that we will be successful in reducing the deficit.
Are weights for the whole Dominion inspected every year ?
Every two years.
Do you find many complaints as to wrong weights and measures ?
No, not many, I think the law has a very good effect. I am inclined to believe that if we give that branch of the service close attention we will succeed in having a first-class service.
Has the hon. gentleman increased the number of inspectors throughout the country ?
No, auite the contrary. In some places I have even refused to make new appointments because I found it was not necessary to do so.

Is there a uniform charge for the inspection of weights and measures ? Are the manufacturers of scales, of whom there are several in the Dominion, charged the same rate as ordinary individuals for inspection ?
Yes, they are charged the same rate.
In the matter of the metric system would the hon. minister explain what success he is meeting with ? The hon. gentleman will remember that last year we had Professor McLennan before the committee.

As to the metric system I last year got a certain sum of money in order to disseminate, to as great an extent as possible, a knowledge of the system throughout the country. We have distributed to high schools and important schools generally metric sets in order to teach the school boys the system. It is now becoming more generally used in the schools of the country and the generation which is now growing up will certainly be au fait with it. I have been in communication with Lord Strathcona on the question, and he has kept me posted as to what is being done in England in that respect. It is not to be forgotten that last year a Bill was introduced into the House of Lords providing for the introduction of the metric system thus rendering the metric system compulsory in England. The Bill passed the House of Lords and was sent to the House of Commons but parliament adjourned before the question was decided by the House of Commons. I think the matter will come this year before the House of Commons in England. I have obtained copies of the Bill and the report of the discussion on the subject in England and I will be very glad to show these to any hon. member who would like to become acquainted with the Bill and discussions which have taken place there.
In pressing for the adoption of the metric system does the hon. minister meet with any opposition from any quarters ?
So far we have had no strong opposition. The only representations which the department has received have been in favour of the adoption of the system.

The hon. minister said that most of the high schools were being supplied with metric sets. Last year the hon. minister was good enough to send to the high school in my county one of the

sets. Where there is a second or third high school in the county will more than one be supplied ?

Certainly ; wherever there is a high school, whether there are several in the county or not it does not make any difference. I would be glad to supply the schools referred to by my hon. friend with one of the sets each.
1 am very much obliged to the hon. minister and I will be glad to make another application to him for sets. '
