speechtext: About two weeks ago I left a letter in the hon. minister's office from the head master of the high school at Gananoque. I have had no answer to it yet. I hope instructions have been given to ship the metric system set which was asked for.
It must have been sent. However, I will inquire into it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I left the letter addressed to the hon. minister with the hon. gentleman's secretary.

It must have been overlooked because I usually answer all letters sent to me.
Rent, fuel, travelling expenses, postage, stationery, &c., for weights and measures, including amount for purchase of standards of the metric system, salaries and other expenses of inspectors, &c., $35,000.
Mr. FOSTER, These are standards for use at Ottawa ; are they ?
Yes.
What do they cost ?
Do you mean the metric system sets ?
Yes.
$8.33 each.
What are these standards ? Are they what you call metric system sets ?
Yes, they are metric system sets which have been imported from France.
How many of these are you purchasing, and what is the idea ?
I am giving one to each higli school.
Are you sending to each school or only to those that apply ?
I am waiting for applications.
The purpose is just to educate the country up to it.
Yes. To put it in the hands of teachers to educate the children attending the schools.
And when you have done the educational work, you are going to introduce the system ?

Nothing has yet been decided as to that, but I suppose it will have to come. If this system is adopted in England, as is likely, I suppose we will have to do the same thing and also if it is adopted in the United States. I spoke of the movement that is going on in England and I may say that in the United States a very strong movement is being made with regard to the introduction of the system there. When it is introduced in England and the United States we will have to follow suit.
You do not propose to get a little ahead of them ?
We have not yet decided as to that.

It is worth thinking about.
Salaries of inspectors of gas and electric light, $25,000.
McLEAN (Queen's, P.E.I.) What fees are chargeable by these inspectors of electric light and gas ?
The average cost per meter is $1 for five years. There is a regular tariff.
Would the minister give us the instructions to the inspectors? What information are they supposed to supply to the department ?

They have to inspect the meters which are brought to be inspected, they have in each office an apparatus to test electric light meters and those who want their meters inspected bring them there. They are inspected and stamped and certificates are given.
Are these fees paid by the consumer or by the company ?

The fee is paid by the owner of the meter in all cases. If there is some difficulty between the contractor and the consumer, and the consumer wants to have his meter inspected, he asks for the inspection, and if there lias been some mistake in favour of the consumer the contractor has to pay for the inspection. The same thing applies to gas meters.
Is any person appointed by the department to instruct these inspectors as to the manner in which they shall perform their duty ?
Yes, instructions are of course issued as to the manner in which the inspection shall be made.
Is there any fixed charge that they can assess the consumer.?

Yes, there is a charge. It is set forth in the Order in Council pass-

ed January 31, 1899. For meters of tlie capacity of ten lights and under, 75 cents ; for meters of ten lights and not exceeding 20, $1.25 ; for meters from 20 to 30 lights, $1.75; for meters from 30 to 45 lights, $2.25 ; for meters from 45 to CO lights, $2.75; for meters from CO to 80 lights, $3 ; for meters from 80 to 100 lights, $3.50. This is for once in five years.
With reference to the item of electric light inspection, I understand that the collectors of excise revenue in small towns are expected to perform that duty.
The collectors simply collect the inspection fees.

Take the case of the town I live in. The inspector lives in Ottawa. Have his expenses to be paid by the parties asking his services if he goes to inspect an electric meter or a number of electric meters at Pembroke ? Are the expenses from here to that town added to the fees ?
No, that is paid by the department.

There is very little information in this blue book based on the reports of the electric light inspectors. Nothing is given as to the amount invested in each plant, the output of gas or electric light. Supposing a man wants to obtain information, for instance as to the amount of machinery and the output of electric light and gas companies, in order that municipalities desiring to go into the ownership of these services can obtain information as to the cost, there is no information of that kind furnished in this report. What I am now asking is whether it would be possible to have a report of the inspectors giving the cost of machinery in the various gas and electric light plants and the output. I do not mean to have them go into details as to the profit and loss because that would be unreasonable, but such a report as I have indicated would be of value to the municipality.

The interference of the department in the question of gas and electric light is simply for the purpose of testing the measures that are used in connected with the gas and electric light ; that is the full scope of the work of our department.
And it is not compulsory ?

Oh yes, it is compulsory, every meter has to be inspected. My bon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) is asking me whether we could not give in cur reports the output of each company and the amount of work which they are doing and all the figures that would be given, say, in a census of those companies. That does not at all pertain to our department. What we have to do is simply to inspect the measures used by those companies. We have no means of ascertaining their output, 54.
their wealth and their revenue. That does not pertain at all to our work, we have simply to test the measures. We test the weights used by a merchant but we are not supposed to find out how much business that man is doing and what he is worth. It is the same with the gas and electric light companies, and I do not think it would be possible, certainly it would be outside the scope of the present Act, to ask for this information because we have no right to get this information from these companies.
Supposing that the inspector found that the meters supplied by the company were of an inferior quality ? Would it be his duty to make a report to the department ?
Yes, it is his duty to report to the department.

Then whose duty would it be to take measures to compel the company to supply proper meters ?
Mr. BRODEUR, The company is notified to see that its gas is purified ; and if it does not do so, it is subject to the penalty.
The verdict is only as to the quality of the gas ?
Yes.
What is the state of the ledger In regard to the electric light inspection ?
The revenue from gas and electric light inspection last year was $50,218.25, and the expenses, $33,426.15.
In these expenses you include everything ?
Yes ; all the expenses in connection with the service.
How does the account stand in weights and measures ?
The expenditures last year were $84,768.82, and the receipts, $66,355.19.

Taking the two together you are about on an even basis. That is satisfactory as far as it goes. I have always had the opinion, and have tried to enforce it, that these are services that ought not to involve the government in any cost. They are business operations in which the revenue ought to be made to cover every expense that is incurred.
Metric system-to provide for the delivery of lectures and the publication of maps, charts, pamphlets, &c., relating to the metric system of weights and measures, $3,000.
Who is going to do the lecturing ?

No lectures have been given yet. My idea last year, when I first asked for this vote, was to send some person to deliver lectures before the various



boards of trade and such bodies as the Canadian clubs throughout the country. Last year I invited Professor McLennan, of Toronto University, to come and deliver a lecture here. He was kind enough to do so, and gave us a very interesting lecture, of which a number of copies have been distributed, and we are frequently asked to have more printed for distribution in the schools. My idea would be to have a small phamplet explanatory of the system prepared and placed in the hands of all the teachers and children in the public schools of the country. We have distributed sets of the metric system among the high schools, and we should distribute these little pamplets among the teachers and children in the lower schools. I think that would tend to popularize the system. As I have said, we may expect in a year or two to introduce and render compulsory the metric system in this country, especially if it is adopted in the countries with which we deal, such as England, the United States and Australia.

My impression is that you would not gain very much from a general distribution of a pamphlet among the school children ; but I think it would be a good idea to distribute instructions on the subject among the teachers, so that they could give it to those who would make some use of it. I should think it would be an excellent idea to distribute among the teachers a pamphlet which would be explicit, definite, and not too long.

That is part of the work I intended to do.
Adulteration of food and fertilizers, and the administration of the Act respecting fraudulent marking, $30,000.
Give us an idea of what is going on in that.

The Adulteration of Food Act provides that food inspectors shall collect samples of food in different parts of the country every time they are so requested by the department. The samples so collected are sent either to the district analyst or to the department in Ottawa to be analysed. The result of the analysis is then published in bulletins, which are distributed to the members, and also published in our annual report. We find that a great many articles are adulterated, and my intention is to pursue a very aggressive policy with respect to these adulterations. For example, last year we had analysed some spices, most of which were found to be adulterated. The same was true with regard to jams and jellies. Samples of liquor were collected and, strange to say, most of them were found to be absolutely pure, except for the addition of a large quantity of water, which is not an adulteration under the Adulteration Act. We find that maple sugar and mapie syrup are adulterated on a very large scale.
What with ?

With all sorts of things. Generally sugar cane and glucose are used, which are adulterations according to the Act, unless the manufacturers state on the label that the article is a compound. In some instances we have taken proceedings to obtain convictions against those violating the law.

Is it not a fact that several establishments in Montreal and other places manufacture very large quantities of what they call maple sugar from cane sugar and so on, which they ship to the old country with the result that the legitimate trade is being ruined?
Mr. BRODEUR, The chief analyst received instructions a few days ago to look into that question. It has been found, as my hon. friend has just said, that manufacturing houses are now making what they call maple sugar, but what has never seen the maple tree. It is my duty to see that these violations of the law are punished, and I intend doing so as early as possible.
We have had an adulteration of Food Act a number of years, can my hon. friend give us an idea as to what progress has been made in purifying the food stuffs of the country?

The publication of the bulletins has had a good effect, but we shall have to follow a more aggressive policy. Last year I found that in spices the adulteration was in some eases simply horrible. I may say the same with regard to jams and jellies, but I must say, to the credit of the manufacturers, that they came to Ottawa to interview the department and agreed to take proper means to prevent adulteration in the future.

Have there been many actions taken under the Act ? Last year, I believe, there was more adulteration than ever. Take for instance this manufacture of so called maple sugar, which has never seen the maple tree. Then take our jams and jellies, according to reports, the adulteration is worse in these than ever before.

I am not ready to admit that the adulteration in jams and jellies is increasing, because I have the formal promise of all the manufacturers-of most of them at all events-that they will cease using glucose in such large quantities. There were strawberry jams manufactured, for instance, which were perfectly innocent of any strawberry. They were made out of apples which were boiled with some salicylic acid and glucose and sometimes hayseeds were used to make the mixture look like strawberry jam.

I am afraid we are making little progress in stamping out this adulter-

ation. Take our white wine vinegar, maple vinegar, and so on, it is well known that most of these are impure. It does seem to me that if a collection were made of these adulterations and the law vigorously applied, you would see a great improvement in a few months. But unless the law be applied vigorously, I am afraid you will not accomplish anything.
My hon. friend drew my attention to the question of adulterated maple sugar. Well, since a few months we have secured five convictions.
That is a start.
I hope it will go on. I am very well disposed to do my best because it is very important that our maple sugar industry should not be ruined.

No doubt the information furnished by the chief analyst is very desirable and useful, but I fear a great deal of labour is spent to very little purpose, because that information does not reach the general public. What system has the minister of distributing the bulletins ? A member of parliament may get two copies and those may be the only ones that will reach his county.

We are giving the bulletins to the members of both Houses and to those who are entitled to the distribution of public documents. More than that we distribute them gratuitously to all those who ask for them and send copies besides to all the vendors of the articles analysed. It would perhaps be better if a more general distribution were made.
How many were distributed last year ?
A thousand copies of each bulletin and twelve bulletins were issued.

This is a matter of great importance, especially to those Arms which are trying their best to give the people a good article. I know of several industries that try to provide pure jams and jellies, but they are handicapped by men who are selling inferior articles at reduced prices. Would it not be wise for the hon. minister to spend a certain amount of money in publishing these bulletins in the weekly or daily papers ?

The suggestion is a good one, but I would not like to accept if off hand, because the publication of these bulletins in the press would cost a great deal of money. I shall however, consider it carefully. Certainly, 12,000 bulletins is a very small number to be distributed throughout the country, and the people whom the information would most interest do not receive the bulletins at all, whereas if the matter appeared in the daily newspapers, it would * 54$
reach those for whom it is intended, and would be of interest to all. I know a gentleman who put $15,000 into an industry of this kind only last year, and already he finds the inferior goods contracting his markets to a very great extent, because they are sold at low prices.
What is the minister's outside machinery for detecting adulteration ?

In each district, we have a food inspector. Instructions are sent to these inspectors, from time to time to collect samples of the goods. Say, for instance, an inspector is instructed to collect samples of maple sugar. From a certain dealer he takes three samples. One of these is left within the vendor and the other two are sent either to the department here, or to the district analyst. And these are analysed.
He only collects samples ns he is instructed to do so ?
Yes. He gets instructions from the department to collect samples of certain articles and he does so.
Are the food inspectors kept busy at that ?
These men, as a rule, are not only food inspectors but excise officers also, and, when not engaged in the collection of food samples, they are attending to other business.

' I see here in the Auditor General's Report entries showing that one Thomas Kidd is a food inspector who is paid $500 salary and $116 for travelling expenses. He has an allowance for rent of office and so on. If he only collects samples as he is instructed to do, it seems to me Mr. Kidd does not do a very large amount of work.
I think his inspection district covers the whole of Ontario, west of Toronto.

But he cannot have done very much to cover that district, because the travelling expenses with which he is charged amount to only $116. That would not carry him very far. It would be interesting to know just how many collections of samples this inspector has made. Does he have to travel to collect these samples ?
Certainly.

The indications are that he did not do much travelling ; and, if not much travelling then not much collecting ; if not much collecting, then he has not done much for his salary, because I see he is confined to this duty.

Many samples have been collected during the year, including a proportion from Mr. Kidd's district. Travelling in that district would not be so expensive as in others covering a larger area. In any

case Mr. Kidd's is a special case ; I think my hon. friend (Mr. Foster) will not And any other food inspectors but have other work to do as excise officers, inspectors of weights and measures or otherwise in connection with the department's work. Mr. Kidd is the only case and I see that he was appointed in 1890.

It is not a question of when he was appointed, but whether the government are spending money and not getting due service for it. The other food inspectors seem to receive small salaries, and I imagine that most of them must do something else.
That is true of all of them except Mr. Kidd. I was saying that he had been appointed many years ago, and 1 suppose that that is the reason he has no other work in connection with the department.
The inspectors seem to go only when they are instructed. Perhaps the minister has not given instructions to Mr. Kidd.	'

Has not the department changed its system within the last few years ? Formerly samples of food for analysis were sent to the department here and the work was done here. But I think that analysts have been appointed for different parts of the country, and samples are now sent to them.

I may explain that it has been found that these food inspectors have not work for the whole year round. They are supposed to work perhaps four or five months and for the rest of the year they -have nothing to do. That is why, in the appointments lately made, we have tried to appoint men as food inspectors who were already in the service as excise officers or inspectors of weights and measures. Take a man in a district where there is only one bonded warehouse ? He can easily absent himself from his place for a few days and attend to the collection of food samples. I see that Mr. Kidd is simply a food inspector. But his territory is a populous one, and, though he does not seem to have travelled much, he has certainly attended to his work in that district, as the chief analyst tells me that he has had samples from that district as from the others.

How does the minister interpret the term ' adulteration of food ? ' The hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) has raised this point as to jam. Suppose an article is put on the market called raspberry jam. If it is in part raspberry jam but with apples used as a filler, would that be considered adulterated ?

Certainly, if it is not marked ' compound.' The law provides that if, on analysis it is found to contain any ingredient injurious to health, it is then de-Mr. BRODEUR.
Glared adulterated. If it is not the pure article, but contains nothing injurious to health, the label must bear the word ' compound ' or the party is liable to be prosecuted for violation of the law. That is the way we proceed with those violations. Take the case of raspberry jams put on the market without containing any raspberries at all. That would certainly be a violation of the Adulteration Act because they have no right to sell an article as raspberry jam if there is no raspberry at all in it.

I am pleased with the interpretation of the minister. But I cannot see where any harm is done to the public when the article used as a substitute in the manufacture of a jam is a good article of food and not in any way detrimental to the people who buy it. Now, Canadian jams that are made and sold on the market are largely made from apple pummace, and then a certain amount of fruit is added in order that it may bear the name of the particular fruit that is stamped on the label. There is no harm at all done to the public who buy that, and I am glad to hear that it is not considered an adulteration where the substitute used is perfectly healthy and not in any way detrimental to any purchaser.

If the substitute replaces absolutely the article which is named on the label, it is an adulteration. Take the ease of strawberry jam. Strawberries are very scarce, and I am informed that instead of using the strawberries they are using turnips. There is no strawberry in it, and it would not be fair to allow such an article to pass without declaring it adulterated. The department declares that when a substitute is made for the genuine article, if it is not marked ' compound,' then the article is declared adulterated. If there is no strawberry in the jam at all it is declared adulterated, even if the foreign fruit is not injurious to public health.
If the package is marked pure raspberry jam and 25 per cent of that is raspberry and the balance is apple, would you call that an adulteration ?
Certainly, the department would declare it an adulteration, because it is sold as pure raspberry jam, whereas 75 per cent of it is not raspberry.

Would it not be well to compel the manufacturer to state on the label the ingredients of which the article is composed ? I do not know if that would be practicable, but it would relieve the public mind to know exactly what the article is composed of. If it was strawberry jam the people would like to know how much strawberry was in it and how much apple-compel the manufacturer to put the ingredients on the label.

I am informed by the chief analyst that it would be very difficult

for manufacturers to comply with that condition. When an article is sold containing ingredients foreign to the article itself, then the manufacturer has to put the word 'compound ' on the label, and the word has to be as prominent as the other words of the label. In that way the manufacturer can comply with the law,.-and that prevents a great deal of adulteration. That is what we are doing at the present time.

With reference to the estimate, 1 do not think it is too large ; in fact I think it would be wise to make it larger, if by so doing you can inform people as to the kind of fruit that is put into the jams they are eating. From what I can learn, in many of the factories throughout the country, to a large extent, jams in particular are made up of most inferior fruits and turnips and glucose, and most inferior grades of these articles. However, I would like to ask, with reference to these bulletins, does the minister mean, when he says that 12,000 bulletins are issued, that each bulletin covers all kinds of food ?

Last year 1,000 bulletins covering each article were issued. We have twelve bulletins issued ; one, for instance, with regard to milk, another with regard to spices, another with regard to jams and jellies, and so on ; 1,000 bulletins regarding each article have been distributed.

The minister must see that only 12,000 bulletins for the whole Dominion would be of very little use. When . you expend $30,000 in obtaining the information. that information is certainly worth distributing far and wide. I would strongly advise the minister to make a still wider distribution of the bulletins.

I am informed that the bulletins are not distributed to newspapers. I think it would be advisable to distribute them to newspapers, and I shall give instructions to that effect. The press usually takes a great deal of interest in these matters, and I think would be glad to publish the information.

If you leave it to the newspapers, they are likely to pick out only such parts as they please and to publish a garbled statement. Would it not be wise for the department to issue a synopsis of the bulletins, and send the synopsis to the newspapers ?
Is it the intention of the department to continue the policy of prosecuting parties who sell goods marked as genuine when they are not genuine ?
We intend to enforce the law rigidly in that respect. Last year I found there were a great number of violations, and we must find means to prevent them if possible.

I may inform the minister that he will find there are very few goods
sold on the market to-day known as jams, for instance, that are pure. The department may go a little too far in that direction. The manufacturers of jams and jellies in this country have to compete with American and English jams, and I doubt if there is any jam sold to-day, either imported or Canadian, that is absolutely pure. For myself, I cannot see where it is detrimental to the public health if apple pulp is used along with other pure fruits. I hope the law will not be interpreted too rigidly in that respect. because it may have the effect of killing a very Important industry in this country.

I may say that my hon. friend is misinformed as to jams imported from England, because by the analysis we made last year we found that the jams imported into this country from England were absolutely pure. But we did not find the same thing in regard to the Canadian and American product. We not only collect samples of the Canadian product but we collect samples of goods which are brought into the country. I must say that it is to the credit of England that the jams and jellies imported from that country which we analysed last year were found to be absolutely pure.

I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Haldimand (Mr. Lalor) in" reference to allowing a certain amount of adulteration. There is no doubt that there is plenty of fruit in our country and there is no excuse for the factories not producing a good pure article. I know there are factories that .are doing their utmost to produce a pure article, and it would be very unsatisfactory so far as they are concerned if any adulteration were permitted.

That would be all right if the department were as watchful in connection with goods imported from England or the United States. If our producers have to compete with outoide manufacturers and if we allow Americans to send goods in here without carefully watching their product it would be a great hardship on our own manufacturers.

House in committee on Bill (No. 34), respecting the Nicola, Kamloops and Similka-meen Coal and Railway Company.
On section 3,
The company, as now organized, is hereby declared to he, and to have been since the pas-

170S
sing of chapter 164 of the statutes of 1903, a body corporate and politic within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, with power to lay out, construct and operate the railway works described in the Acts of the province of British Columbia mentioned in the preamble, and with all the other powers therein set forth, so far as the legislative powers of the parliament of Canada extend, save and except only such provisions of the said Acts, if any, as are inconsistent with the Railway Act, 1903 ; but nothing herein contained shall affect or invalidate any action heretofore taken by the company pursuant to powers in the said Acts contained. .

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Is that the date of the Provincial Act ?

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes, this is the Bill that went to a sub-committee and the committee accepted the report of the sub-committee.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It seems to me that it raises a very important question. If there is a provincial Act, and litigation should arise under the provisions of the provincial Act, the fact that we are now declaring that from the time that Act was passed in the province the railway was a work for the general advantage of*Canada, we are practically bringing it under federal jurisdiction and authority, and difficulty might arise. We would seem to be deliberately interfering with the powers of the province.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The Bill was carefully considered in committee ; it also went to a subcommittee.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I was a member of the subcommittee which considered this Bill. The conditions are very peculiar as I remember it. In the first place in 1891 an Act was passed by the British Columbia legislature incorporating this company. In 1S93 the company came to this House . asking that this work be declared for the general advantage of Canada, but when they came here a question was raised as to whether or not the charter granted in 1891 had expired under the provision of the General Railway Act of British Columbia, which required that they should do a certain amount of work at a certain time, which had not been done. When this was brought to the attention of the House in 1903, there was a stay of proceedings until the British Columbia House had passed another Act reviving the old charter. On the receipt of a telegram from the British Columbia legislature stating that this Act had been passed, this parliament, in 1903, passed an Act declaring this work to be for the general advantage of Canada. When they came to get the Bill which was passed in 1903 by the British Columbia legislature, they found that it contained a clause which took the control of the rates out of the power of the Railway Commission and gave it to the Governor in Council of British Columbia. The question was then raised Mr. BARR.
whether it was not ultra vires of the legislature of British Columbia to pass that Act, and consequently there has been some question with reference to the validity of the bonds of this company. Now as they desire to extend the line to a point on the Vancouver, Victoria and Eastern Railway, they come to parliament and aak us to pass this Act to validate their bonds and so remove any doubts about the British Columbia Act.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It may be that the province of British Columbia gave a subsidy and in consideration thereof reserved to themselves the right to control freight rates, but now we declare the work to be for the general advantage of Canada and bring it under the Dominion Railway Act. The rates on railways under the Dominion Railway Act are controlled by a commission, so that we take the power which the legislature reserves to themselves away from them, although they reserved it probably for a consideration. That is sometimes done as in the case of the agreement between the legislature of Manitoba and the Canadian Northern Railway. The legislature reserved the right to control freight rates in consideration of guaranteeing the bonds of the railway. In such a case, if we should declare the railway to be for the general advantage of Canada and thereby bring it under the General Railway Act, we certainjy would be con-liicting with their power to control freight rates, and the question would arise whether the provincial authorities or the Railway Commission would control' the rates. The same question may be involved here.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
The company has already, by the Act of 1903, been declared for the general advantage of Canada. Therefore this Bill does not affect it so far as that goes. But they ask us under this Bill for power to extend this road to connect with the Vancouver, Victoria and Eastern Railway at or near Grand Forks, and at or near Midway with the Columbia and Western Railway. We amend the second clause to read :
All powers of the company in relation to tha railway which it now has authority to construct shall extend and apply to the extension authorized in section 1 of this Act.
I admit that it is a very much mixed up piece of legislation, but at the same time, as far as declaring it for the general advantage of Canada is concerned, that has been already done in 1903, in regard to the main portion of the road, and this is only continuing	to the extension	of that
road the same provisions as were made in the Act of 1903. There did not seem to be any objection to the Bill ; there were some British Columbia members present at the meeting of the sub-committee, but there did: not seem to be any opposition coming from

British Columbia with reference to this matter.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not know if they got any subsidy from British Columbia and if in lieu of that, the legislature retained in their hands the right to control the rates. 1 think that before the Bill is read the third time is should be submitted to the Minister of Justice or some competent authority connected with the government to look into it and see that we are not infringing on rights belonging to the province.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
It is quite clear that we are not doing that because the amending words qualify that meaning.
So far as the legislative powers of the parliament of Canada extend.
We are declaring that the company shall continue to enjoy the powers it now enjoys by authority of its provincial Act so far as the legislative powers of the parliament of Canada extend. We do not purport to legislate in any way beyond our own powers. It is possible that a province may be able to legislate with regard to a local work to a greater extent than we can. Therefore, we do not purport by this amendment to ratify any powers granted by the provincial Act in excess of those powers which this parliament can grant.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: This brings the freight rates under the control of the Railway Commission.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: All railways subject to this parliament are under the control of the Railway Act.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: If we control the freight rates, how can the province ?

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: It cannot. The moment it becomes a Dominion railway, it comes within the Railway Act. However, the lion. gentleman's suggestion that the third reading should stand over is not unreasonable.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The point involved in this Bill is that this railway having been declared one for the general advantage of Canada, it declares that from the date of the passage of the Bill providing for that the company owming the railway has corporate rights and powers. This parliament alone is seized with the jurisdiction to deal with this railway in this declaratory way. That is the view of the subcommittee, and that view was shared by the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale), who drafted the amendment- made to the third clause, and by the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron), who were members of that committee.

subsubtopic: NICOLA, KAMLOOPS AND SIMILKAMEEN COAL AND RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not think it is competent for us to take over any provincial railway and destroy any rights the province
has in it by saying that it is for the general advantage of Canada. That is a question of law to be determined ultimately by the courts. We have had that question before this House again and again, and there seem to be no decisions that touch directly upon it. We may be within our rights or we may not. If we are within our rights, we may be interfering with the rights that properly belonged to the province when it originally granted the charter for this railway.
