House in Committee of Supply.
Adulteration of food and fertilizers, and the administration of the Act respecting fraudulent marking, 530,000.

Before this item passes, I wish to say a few words with reference to the fruit industry. In the northern part of my riding we have one of the most promising fruit districts to be found in the province of Ontario. Situated as it is at the southern end of Lake Huron, it is generally conceded to have equal advantages to those of the Niagara district. Hence
1	think it is important that this matter
should be gone into a little more fully. When we have proper transportation facilities and proper protection, I am satisfied that the fruit industry of our country will grow and increase as it should. Thousands of barrels of apples rotted under the trees in my riding during the last season simply because the transportation facilities were not what they should be, and because the protection to Canadian fruit was not sufficient to prevent fruit coming in from foreign countries. With reference to the adulteration of jams and jellies to which reference has been made, I would like to call the minister's attention to bulletin 96 of the Inland Revenue Department for 1903, which states that the analysis of jams and jellies selected indiscriminately over the Dominion showed the following results :	raspberry jam-genuine
2	; doubtful 1; adulterated, 16 ; total 19. Strawberry jam,-genuine, one; doubtful, one ; adulterated, 17. Total, 19. Plum jam, -genuine, 3 ; doubtful, 1 ; adulterated, 8. Total, 12. Peach jam,-genuine, none ; doubtful, 2 ; adulterated, 5. Total, 7. Miscellaneous,-genuine, none ; doubtful, none ; adulterated, 2. Jellies,-genuine, 8 ; doubt-

ful, none; adulterated, 7. Showing that out of 74 varieties, only 14 were genuine. When we consider that the adulteration to a large extent is by means of turnips, which can be purchased at about $6 a ton, I am sure the hon. minister will readily see the importance of making a more thorough investigation of this subject than he has done. As regards the distribution of the bulletins, I wish to again impress on the hon. minister the importance of a more genera] distribution, and of giving to the public a short synopsis at least of the analysis of the jams and fruits that are canned in our country, showing the results of their analysis. And also information regarding the quantity brought into the country from outside. Take for instance canned preserves, jellies, jams, &c., there were imported in nine months, in 1904, $147,256 worth, or about $200,000 worth of these goods coming to our country per annum. 1 sincerely trust that the hon. minister will try and provide a remedy for this. We can grow the finest fruits in this country, and it has been proven within the last year that a great quantity of our fruits never reached the market and are not likely to so long as this heavy importation goes on. Take for instance the green fruits imported into Canada, in 1903 they amounted in value to $1,033,115, leaving out of question the dried fruits. I merely call the hon. minister's attention to these matters in order to impress upon him the importance of having the bulletins showing the adulteration of food distributed more largely, and also of making more public the amount of foreign goods in this line that are coming into our country.

As regards the adulteration of raspberry and strawberry jams, as I explained this afternoon, we collected samples last year and found in many instances that there were violations of the Adulteration Act. In some instances the berries were not used at all and glucose was used instead of sugar. With regard to the imports, of course, in the amount mentioned by my hon. friend are included fruits, such as bananas and oranges which are not grown in this country, and dried fruits.
I did not include any dried fruits.

In any event I have no control over the importation of these goods as we cannot prevent their importation by the application of the Adulteration Act. We intend to take an aggressive policy with regard to the carrying out of this law and to spread the information among the public of the results of the analysis, so that the people may know whether the goods they are buying are genuine or not.

Would it be too much to ask the hon. gentleman to ex-Mr. ARMSTRONG.
elude vegetables altogether out of the jams and jellies made in our country ?
Did you find any turnips in them ?
We did not discover any vegetables.
They have been found, it is Said, by the analysts.

Before this item passes, I wish to refer to two or three things that have been impressing themselves on my mind while listening to this discussion. In the first place, we are spending $30,000 per year, and it does not seem as if we were getting an adequate result in so far as the two chief things are concerned-first, the punishing of those who are guilty, and secondly, the dissemination of the results of these analysis by the department so that the people might be educated, and thus a general interest of self protection aroused which would help the department to get rid of these adulterators. You have an analytical department at Ottawa which costs $8,000 or $9,000 per year and which seems to be pretty well equipped, then you have outside resident analysts in the different cities who are available for the purpose of analysing the samples of food which may be put into their hands. You further have your inspector of food to whom a certain amount of money is paid, both as salary and travelling expenses. I suppose a good deal of analysis is done at the request of persons who send samples to the headquarters at Ottawa.
Yes, to some extent.
That they do simply for their own information. Are they charged a fee ?
Yes.

Well, that does not amount to much. A man thinks there is adulteration and sends the sample for his own satisfaction, pays his fee, gets the analysis and uses it for whatever it is worth. But the analysing that is done for the purpose of detecting and punishing the adulteration of food is done mainly at the head office and by these local analysts. No less a sum than $30,000 is spent.
We did not spend as much last year.

Well, that is the vote you are taking.
Mr. BRODEUR, Last year a vote was taken for $30,000 and we spent $20,900.

Then the minister did not do his duty last year, because we have had him acknowledging to-night that there is a great deal of adulteration. When parliament gave him $30,000 to detect and prevent adulteration, he sat down quietly and

only spent $20,000 of it. There is an economy which is laudable, but there is another which, in the face of a grave danger like this, is just the opposite. The aggressiveness which my hon. friend speaks about animated him but very little last year since he did not even spend the money put at his disposal.
I was only there a few months.

What I spoke of refers to the department. Is the department doing what it ought to do with reference to these analysts in outside cities ? It gives a retaining fee of $200 and an allowance for office rent, apparatus and material, of about as much more. There is an initial expense of about $400 in each case. You have these analysts in Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Victoria, Quebec, London, Winnipeg and Ottawa. When you incur this initial expense, it seems to me poor economy not to utilize the staff you thus retain. Now, what does the department do? In Halifax the officer retained analysed only 60 or 70 samples ; in Montreal about the same ; in Toronto about the same ; in Victoria only 26. In Quebec there was the initial expense, yet not a single analysis was made, so that the money spent was absolutely useless. In London only 9 samples were analysed. In Winnipeg the samples analysed number only 28. In Ottawa they gave the retaining fee, the office rent, the allowance for apparatus and material, yet did not call upon Dr. Valade to analyse a single sample during the year. Now, if these are the facts-and I suppose it will not be denied

we see that the department went to large expense to retain men and provide apparatus and material for the analysis of food, yet had not sprawl enough to have analyses actually made. And yet adulteration is rife in this country, as the minister has acknowledged He says he is determined to make an aggressive campaign against it. But though these manufacturers have been adulterating food, and are still adulterating, the department has not used, to any great extent, the apparatus and men at its disposal for the prevention of this adulteration. Then as to the food inspectors, the same remark applies. The department incurs the initial expense for salary and fees. It lets these officers travel a little, but not enough to collect many samples. There is a yearly expense of about $4,000 for these officers, yet the number of samples they have collected is very small. The minister will see what I am driving at-that if he is going to continue spending $20,000 in this kind of thing and have an establishment, he ought to go further and make his Initial expenditure effective, even if a little more money must be spent. The minister now is like a gentleman who has an immense battery and with ammunition ready, but never loading or firing his guns, though the enemy are there and ready to be slaughtered-and deserving to be slaughtered, as he himself admits. This is a friendly criticism, and it is spoken in the hope that the minister will utilize the machinery he has provided to put down the great evil of adulteration of food. As to the education part of it, the distribution of 1,000 copies of each of twelve bulletins will not do it at all. Could not more of these be sent out with a view to arousing public interest ? No man wants to buy food that is adulterated and not worth the money that he pays for it. Yet nineteen-twentieths of the people have no idea but that they are buying good food. One way to get rid of adulteration is to arouse the intelligent interest of the consuming people to the fact that they are buying food that is either injurious or not worth what it costs them. The minister will do something now with the newspapers. I think that is a good move. An idea that suggested itself to me was that members of the House would probably be glad to assist in this distribution. If members knew that these bulletins were available for distribution, many would be glad to make up lists of people in their constituencies to whom they would like to send things, and who would be interested in the facts contained in these documents. In that way two or three hundred people might be reached in every constituency, and, with over two hundred members of the House taking an interest in it, the distribution would be very wide and, probably, very effective. Then the schools might be utilized and the boards of trade might be utilized. I should think that secretaries of boards of trade would be glad to distribute these bulletins. The best of trade is honest trade, and, beyond doubt, legitimate traders would be in favour of stopping adulteration and, in the general interest of trade, have nothing sold purporting to be pure food that was not actually pure. For my part, I have no objection to men selling or buying a mixed article, provided it is not sold under a false name. I believe that the prevention of adulteration of food is one of the most important subjects we can take up among the minor subjects in connection with our public policy. We had a discussion the other day on the prevention of tuberculosis. The carrying out of the reform in that direction would save life. The prevention of the sale of adulterated food saves life and promotes health. If the government is going to take this matter up at all, it ought to take it up with energy and purpose. It ought to terrify the evil-doer and arouse the victims to a sense of what is going on in the way of dissimulating, under false names, what I dare say in many cases are very noxious articles of food.

I am glad that this discussion is taking place with regard to the adulteration of food. When I came into the department, I tried to acquaint myself as much as possible with this question, and

became much interested in it, and I have ever since been studying the best means of carrying out this very important law. There is no doubt that the adulteration of food is a very serious evil in this country. I trust that it is being gradually lessened, but at the same time if we do not continue to put forth efforts to stamp it out, it will become very serious again. I understand how important it is that we should take every means to prevent this evil spreading. My hon. friend has mentioned the fact that very few samples have been sent to our district analysts during the last year, and he argues therefrom that we have not done our duty. He must not forget, however, that most of the analyses, perhaps seventy-five per cent of the analyses that have been made during the past year, were made at the head office in Ottawa, instead of being made by the district analysts. It has been found very convenient indeed to have the analyses made here instead of by the district analysts, who are generally occupied with their own business. Take for example a doctor who has to look after his clients, he cannot devote the time which he ought to take in making an analysis of the samples which are sent to him. Perhaps some other analysts are in the same position. Then it has frequently been found that it was better to send the samples here to be analysed by the head office in Ottawa. Moreover, we have in many instances found different results from analyses made of the same article in different parts of the country; an analysis in the west may not give the same results as an analysis in the east though the article is the same. There is another thing to be considered, and which has been pressed upon my attention. Some of these officers do not devote much time to that business, and occasionally they get the analysis done by some one else. ' But we have to pay these district analysts a certain amount for each sample they analyse, besides the retaining fee which is given them. This makes it very expensive, much more expensive than to have the same samples analysed by our officers in Ottawa. The analysis made here does not cost anything, because the officers are paid a yearly salary; Mr. McGill, for instance, gets $1,800 or $2,000, and some others a lesser amount. So the Auditor General's Report does not give a fair idea of the number of samples which have been analysed during the year, because a great many other analyses are made besides those made by the district analysts. I have already mentioned that about seventy-five per cent of all the samples are analysed here at the head office of which no record is made in the Auditor General's Report. 1 may repeat what I have already said, that I intend to pursue a very aggressive policy with regard to the adulteration of foods, i have had several communications with boards of trade and with the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, which latter organization Mr. BRODEUR.
is taking a great deal of interest in this question. They have been good enough to mention the fact in their reports that we are trying to do our best to repress this evil, and it is my intention to pursue that policy rigorously.

That is all right so far as it goes, and that brings me to what I had in my mind but did not speak of before. You never can get as authoritative-an analysis from one of your district analysts as you can from your central authority here. You must be better equipped here than any district analyst can be, with all your skill, and your knowledge, and your accumulation of experience. If I were living in a distant part of Canada and wanted an analysis made, I would send the sample to the central office here rather than to the local analyst, who might be busy with his own affairs. Then there is the cost of transporting all these samples back and forth, there is constant communication between them and Ottawa. Why in the world with your central laboratory here in Ottawa, should you pay a retaining fee to the district analysts and these allowances, with $100 rent for the office, and his apparatus, and cost of material, when you have right under your nose, in your own central organization, ail these things much better equipped ? The amount that you spend on these men far distant for retaining fees would more than pay ail the expenses of transit of your samples from these distant parts here to Ottawa, and the communications that take place. It seems to me the best method would be to abolish all these outside offices, whose work can only be partial and ineffective, and cannot have the authority of the central analysis. Do all your analyses at the central laboratory, and you would thereby save a good deal of money which now seems to be spent without much result. I am not saying anything against these district analysts. This practice has grown up with time. A man is justified in taking a retaining fee if he finds a department which is willing to give it to him. But the whole question is, having so much money, what is the best way to expend it, and it does not seem to me it is the best way, while you have a properly equipped laboratory here and able to do the work, that you should have these outlying offices where the business must be indifferently well done under the best circumstances, and where little of the work is done.

With regard to these district analysts, I am inclined to take very much the same view as the hon. gentleman. In fact I may mention that several vacancies have occurred during the last year that we have not found it advisable to fill. In Quebec, for instance, I think the analyst has resigned and he has not been replaced, the analyst in St. Hyacinthe has not been

replaced, so also in Winnipeg. I think there are four vacancies now.
I would make about five more.

Well, it is very hard sometimes to dismiss men who have been for many years in the service. Take Dr. Valade here in Ottawa, I think he has been nearly twenty-five years in the service. Perhaps the time has not arrived to do that, particularly since some of these men were appointed before this government came into power. I will take into consideration the suggestion that has been made. The hon. gentleman sees what I have done so far. I have refused to replace officers although I was pressed in several instances to do so when vacancies occurred for that very reason. I have not had much experience, because I have been only a short time in the department, but I am inclined to the belief that the suggestion which has been made by the hon. gentleman is absolutely correct and it is one which I have followed in so far as vacancies are concerned.
If my hon. friend does not wish to act harshly with these officers keep them at work until they die.
But they cost money.
They do.
Suppose that instead of sending samples to Mr. Macfarlane we sent them to Dr. Valade, we would have to pay Dr. Valade for each sample analysed. It is better to have them analysed by Mr. Macfarlane.

I would like to endorse everything that has been said by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) in regard to the centralization of these samples. In the medical profession we adopt a rule like that in almost every province. I know that in my own province we do. While medical men, of later years, are equipped with the microscope and a great many of them make a study of bacteriology, yet the best and nicest way is to send to the provincial bacteriologists for our analysis. In cases of diphtlieretie membrane and in the finer tests of urinalysis, we do not depend on the microscope or the tests of individual members of the profession however well we may think of our ability, because we know that at the central office greater expense has been gone to with the object of providing finer and nicer instruments and better results are obtained. I think that in the case of adulterated foods which is one of the most important questions that this House can consider, a question that affects the health of almost every family that buys these foods- and tons and tons are bought every year- it is very important that steps should be taken to find out to what extent adulteration is practised, and I am sure that no better
step could be taken than by centralizing this service and providing it with the finest equipment that can be obtained. The adoption of this plan would make the service much more effective and better in every way.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to put one or two questions to the hon. minister of Inland Revenue in connection with this item. The first one I would like to ask is how it is that so many analyses are made of products obtained from retail dealers when the department could attack the fountain head and find out what was in these foods without having to go to thousands and tens of thousands of retailers throughout the country ? The factories that turn out jams are very few in number, they can be counted on the fingers of one hand, or at most of two hands. Eight or ten analyses would show what these jams contain. Why should each retailer who is selling the products of these factories, the contents of which he does not know, be subjected to this analysis and test when the analysis could just as well be made of the article when it leaves the. factory ? It has the maker's name on it. The maker should be held responsible for the ingredients that are in the article named. Take the question of spices, for instance ; spices are generally put up in cans or packages. The man who puts them up is the man who should know what they contain. If he does not know he does not know his business. Why should every retailer throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion be subjected to having his spices analysed, when the number of dealers in spices could be counted on the fingers of one's hand, or two hands ? Why should a thousand or ten thousand samples be taken and analysed when by going to the makers or those who mix or produce these spices the whole thing could be shut off at the fountain head ? It appears to me that the department covers too wide a field in endeavouring to shut off the stream at its outlet instead of endeavouring to shut it off at its source, because it is a well known fact that the principal place at which adulteration takes place is the factory. As to the matter of jams, this is a subject, of course, which is rather sweet, but to return to them I would like to ask the hon. minister if the basis of jam is turnips or carrots, it is classed as adulterated under the laws that govern the department. I think I am in a position to state" that the basis of American jams is the articles named. Turnips particularly constitute the basis of jams. The turnip" is a harmless article, but any one can see that when jams are sold at seven cents a pound, as they are mostly, they must be constituted of something other than fruit and sugar, because the labour, the package that contains the jam and the fruit and sugar cannot be brought together, put into the package and sold for seven cents a pound.

i
It is a self-evident fact that there is something else besides fruit and sugar in the jam that brings down the price. I have been consulting the returns in regard to the export of turnips which go to prove that in American factories these articles enter largely into the production of jams. During the past year there were exported from Canada, 1,085,000 bushels of turnips of a value of $107,000. Of this quantity, 1,067,000 bushels went to the United States. These, I am informed and I think correctly informed, are sent almost invariably to the jam factories of the United States. That may be a lamentable fact, but nevertheless I believe it is a fact. Now, we re-import from the United States a large quantity of jam and jellies, which, no doubt, to a considerable extent, contain these ingredients. I would like to ask the hon. minister, if, when these goods are analysed, the fact that they contain turnips or carrots is sufficient to bar them as adulterated foods. They are certainly not what they are represented to be, and if they are not what they are represented to be it would appear to be the duty of the department, if they want to put into general use only pure foods, to stop all goods that will not pass the test at the border. They should not be allowed to come into the country. You should not then attack the retail dealer who perhaps had nothing to do with the importation, who has had nothing to do with the making of them and who is not able to tell of what they are constituted. Therefore, I submit this proposition that any adulteration that takes place in the country takes place in the factory or the institution that puts up these goods or manufactures them. That is one point. The next point is that if it is sought to bring into the country articles which are impure, the proper place to stop them is at the border line. They should not be allowed to come into the country, but they should be stopped when they are being imported. That would not then throw the onus upon thousands and ten thousands of retail dealers throughout Canada when they actually do not know what the goods contain and who cannot correctly find out without going to a great deal of trouble. I submit these points to the hon. gentleman's attention. 1 believe that these are facts. If they are not, I would like him to point out to me wherein I have misstated the facts. I hope that in the future the department will attend more to confining their efforts to the source of the trouble instead of attacking the various branches of trade. 1 think the hon. gentleman would be conferring a great benefit upon the trade of the country if he would prohibit factories that offend against the law by manufacturing that class of food and turn it out, although they do it under a false name, rather than attack the retailer who is perfectly innocent and knows nothing about the contents. He is the man who generally has to suffer and Mr. COCKSHUTT.
the manufacturer seems to escape. I commend these points to the hon. gentleman's attention, and I hope he will reply to them.

With regard to the collection of samples from the retailers and the wholesalers, I agree, to a certain extent, with the remarks made by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cockshutt). I gave instructions some time ago that in future we should collect these samples on a larger scale from the manufacturers and the wholesalers. We find, however, a very great difficulty in obtaining samples from the manufacturers. They do not pretend to have them for sale, and we have some difficulty in collecting samples from them, but the suggestion made is certainly a good one, and I think that instead of going only to the retailers, we should also collect samples, when it is possible, from the manufacturers and the wholesalers, because if we succeed ill impressing upon the manufacturer the fact that if he sells adulterated goods it will he published broadcast ; then, I suppose, he will become much more anxious to sell only pure goods. We must, at the same time, remember that the wholesalers are not absolutely free from blame, because it happens sometimes that after the goods have left the hands of the wholesalers or manufacturers, they are mixed up with other materials, and the retailer then becomes responsible ; but we must not forget that when we collect samples from the retailer, he gives us the name of the manufacturer, which, as my hon. friend may see in the report which he has before him, is also published. If the manufacturer has sold adulterated goods to the retailer, he is exposed to having his name published as it is in that bulletin. It has been said also that turnips are used on a large scale in the manufacture of jams. The chief analyst informs me that he has never found any turnips in the goods that he has analysed. I do not pretend to say that they are not used.
Does he say that in goods either from the United States, Canada or Great Britain, he has never found any turnips ?
What we have found is particularly apple pulp instead of strawberries or raspberries.
But in the jams ?

It is apple pulp which the chief analyst informs me he has found most in the jams that are adulterated. At the same time, this is certainly a violation of the law, because when I buy strawberry jam I am supposed to have strawberries, and if, instead of finding strawberries, I simply find apple pulp, to which has been added salicylic acid, coal tar dye and some other things like that, it is certainly a violation of the law. Jam is supposed to contain fruit, sugar and water, and

we sometimes find glucose instead of sugar, eoal tar dye, salicylic acid and apple pulp. It is a very serious thing that manufacturers should put on the market goods in that condition, and even try to sell those goods as pure strawberry jam. I think the time has arrived when we should adopt an aggressive policy to prevent such things being sold in the future.
With regard to the turnips, it was to the American trade particularly that I referred, not to the Canadian packers. I am not in a position to state what Canadian packers use.

If we have samples directly from the wholesalers, I think we would reach that violation of the law. Thai is why I thought, in order to reach the source of the evil, we should go to the manufacturer and the wholesaler.
I thought my hon. friend told us there were no roots or turnips in the jams analysed ?
I thought my hon. friend referred to the goods manufactured in this country. I do not know that they are using turnips in the United States.

I would like to ask the minister how he manages in connection with imported jams, catsups, &c., from the United States ? How do you treat them in regard to adulteration ? I may say that the gentlemen who are talking about turnips in jams are not very well posted in the jam business. I think that when the minister tells us that apple pulp is more generally used, he is nearer the truth than the gentlemen who talk of turnips.
We simply reach them in the same way as we reach the Canadian product; an American sample is just as liable to be condemned and declared adulterated as a Canadian.

I think it is a most unfortunate thing for us in this country to put the screws on the Canadian manufacturers and allow the Americans to bring in goods that are not pure. We thought we had it from the minister that there were no I'oots found in the American importations that were analysed. I understand from a good authority that the Americans are using roots, and that they are underselling our Canadian manufacturers in different lines of this business, with the result that the Canadians are almost going out of the business, whilst the Americans are sending in their impure goods. I contend that the importations, even from the British islands, and particularly from the United States, should be very carefully analysed, and it should be placed beyond a doubt that we are not receiving from the American, side, competing with our manufacturers, impure goods'; imported goods should be eyen more carefully analysed than those manufactured in this country.
What is the result of the examination of goods from foreign countries ?

As far as jams and jellies are concerned, as I said this afternoon. all the goods which were imported from Great Britain were found genuine. The chief analyst informs me that there were very few samples of American goods which were sent to be analysed, and in fact his impression is that there is a very small quantity of American jam used.
Have many American goods been carefully examined ?

A few were analysed. The chief analyst is not very sure whether some have been examined, but, at all events, we have collected samples, and where we find American goods we certainly buy them to get them analysed just as we do the Canadian product.

Let me call the minister's attention to the fact that $49,000 worth of these goods came from the United States. If only a very small quantity of these were analysed, it is very unfair to analyse the Canadian products so strictly. I might also call the minister's attention to the fact that of the $30,000 voted last year for the purpose of gathering and distributing information over $9,000 was not expended. Would it not be wise, after gathering the information, to spend part of that money in distributing it broadcast ? Then, I might ask the hon. minister if the officers of his department have the privilege of going into any factories in the country and examining food products ?
Mr. BRODEUR, Yes. The chief analyst has visited several factories in this country, and has also attended some congresses outside in order to meet American chemists and get information from them on the important question of analysing food products.

I am sorry that the hon. Minister of Customs is not in his place tonight when this interesting discussion is going on. I believe the chief cause of this trouble about adulteration is that there is not sufficient duty placed on the goods that are imported into Canada. If you sit down at almost any hotel table in this country, you will find that the catsup on that table is imported from the United States ; and the same thing applies largely to all other 'table condiments. That applies even more to the west than it does to the east. If the government will place a much higher duty on these American goods and then enforce the law against adulteration, I believe the Canadian manufacturers will be only too glad to give the Canadian people better and purer articles.

If my hon. friend refers to the figures of the census, I think he

will find that the quantity of these goods imported does not at all compare with the quantity produced in the country. I know that considerable quantities are imported into the Northwest and British Columbia, but a very small quantity is imported into the eastern provinces, where the fruits are produced.

I may inform the hon. minister that over $200,000 worth of this class of goods were imported last year. Not one dollar's worth of these goods should be imported. They should be made in Canada, and they can be if the government will put a sufficient tariff on them.

I would like to ask the minister a few questions. How many collectors in the employ of the department are giving their entire time to the collection of samples of articles supposed to be adulterated ?
There is only one who is devoting all his time to that work. The others are excise officers. We have ten food inspectors.
What is this man's name ?
Thomas Kidd.
Are the samples collected by Mr. Kidd and the others who are partial inspectors, examined locally, or are they sent to the central bureau here ?
Most of the samples collected last year were sent to the central office here.
Are the legal processes in regard to the adulteration of food initiated from here and carried on from here ?
Yes, instructions are given from the department here to take proceedings.
How many proceedings have been taken during the past year ?

No actions have been taken, but a large number of persons whose goods have been found to be adultered have paid the penalty imposed upon them. That penalty generally consists in the payment of the cost of the analysis, besides which we publish their names in the bulletin with the statement that their goods are adulterated. If they do not pay the cost of the analysis, then proceedings are instituted against them.
About what is the cost of the analysis ?
From $11 to $20.

I certainly agree with the hon. member for North Toronto in advocating the strengthening of this department. With its present inadequate staff it seems to me that no work of a far-reaching character can be undertaken. Appar-Mr. BRODEUR.
ently the work is left in a large measure to the local municipalities, who are only able to make prosecutions when they can prove that the food which has been analysed by them contains something deleterious to public health, which is very difficult to prove. For this reason the local authorities are unable to proceed. The work of protecting the public against fraud in the way of adulterations should be carried on chiefly by the Inland Revenue Department, but that department is very inadequately equipped for the great work it has to do. Looking over the reports which have come from the various analysts located at Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, Victoria and elsewhere, I find that there are practically but three substances which these local analysts have analysed-fertilizers, syrup and milk.
The analysing of fertilizers may be very useful, but does not create protection to the public health, and it is a work which seems to me to belong more especially to the Department of Agriculture. As for the analysis of milk, most of our cities are provided with a better way for detecting impure milk than the government of Canada. In Montreal we have a perfectly adequate system and I think that our local board of health looks after this very carefully and thoroughly. I would commend to the hon. minister, if he has not already adopted the system, to follow the same system in obtaining samples for the department. Our inspectors in Montreal are authorized when they suspect that milk which is being sold or about to be sold is adulterated, to stop the vendor, take a certain quantity of milk from his can and put it into two bottles, which are then sealed in such a manner that the seal cannot be tampered with.. One bottle is left with the milkman and the other is brought to the department and analysed. If it is found that the milk is below standard, the case is taken into court, and if the accused is not satisfied with the verdict, he is entitled to produce his own bottle and have a second analysis made. It generally turns out that the second analysis is identical with the first, so that he is practically self convicted. There is a great amount of adulteration in many articles of food at present in Canada, as we have discovered through our local analyses in the board of health at Montreal. For example, large quantities of candies are sold which are coloured by matter that may not be injurious, but certainly is not helpful to public health. We have made frequent analyses of ketchups, and have found that almost any ketchup analysed would stain a cloth which was placed in it, showing that it must contain dye stuff of some character, which is certainly not good for the human system. Other analyses of food stuffs are of a similar character, but being only a local board we have found it very difficult to proceed against those who sold the adulterated goods unless we were prepared to prove that the adulteration rendered the com-

modifies injurious to the public health. Therefore, I would point out to the hon. minister that he has a very large field in which to operate, and if he can see his way clear to strengthen his department so that he may have inspectors to visit all parts of Canada and inspect not only the goods in process of manufacture but also samples of the goods in the packages, he will be conferring a great benefit on the community. Goods in the process of manufacture could be inspected by the same methods I have described in the ease of milk. Goods in packages bearing the name of the maker carry their own identification. I do not think there is any department that calls at present more lolidly for adequate enlargement so that the health of the people may be protected.

There is one subject to which I would like to call the attention of the hon. minister and which I think is germane to the subject in hand. I refer to patent medicines. This country is infested with patent medicines more or less good. Is there any inspection of these when they are put on the market at first or are they inspected now and then? I have a case in mind which happened in the latter days of December in Montreal of some people who were almost poisoned by a medicine called Steam's headache powders. These powders are sold freely to any one who wants to Buy them in all the drug stores. They are, I Believe a most injurious medicine. They are supposed to be a very quick remedy for headaches, and must contain, I imagine, some very strong ingredients, and probably some poison. It is well that we should be very particular about the food we buy, but we should be still more particular about the medicines sold to the people and take some precautions to see that no medicine is likely to have a very injurious effect on those who use it. I would ask my hon. friend what protection, if any, he is prepared to give the public against patent medicines, which instead of doing good are doing harm ?

There has been some agitation amongst physicians to have the packages or bottles containing patent medicines stamped with the formula of its contents. I may tell my hon. friend that there is a great difference of opinion on that point. We have the doctors on the one side and the druggists on the other. The druggists claim that that would be injurious to their trade. We are entitled under the law to collect samples of drugs and we do it very frequently, and when drugs are adulterated the same course is followed with regard to them as with regard to food.

I know that the doctors and druggists are not at one on that question. Many doctors are opposed to patent medicines and would rather give their own remedies, but the druggists find a great profit in selling those medicines. But since
my hon. friend has all the machinery requisite in his department, would it not be possible for his chief analyst to have patent medicines collected and analysed and declare whether they are injurious or the reverse ?

I am informed by the chief analyst that it would be very difficult to do that, so far as patent medicines are concerned, because as long as they correspond with the specifications it is almost impossible to declare them adulterated.
Would it not be possible to find out whether they are pure or adulterated before they are freed from the customs and when the entry is being made to take them out of customs?

That might perhaps be a good plan, but it would require an army of officers connected with all the different ports to inspect samples of all the goods entered, I am sure it would be a very costly experiment.

Has the department had any analyses made of fertilizers in New Brunswick? There are very serious complaints regarding the quality of fertilizers sold in that province. I have heard it said that farmers are very frequently defrauded, and if the department has any power to apply a remedy in the matter I would like to see that power exercised.

Under the law persons selling fertilizers are obliged to have them analysed every year, sending samples to the office here for that purpose. I should be surprised to learn that fertilizers are sold that are not being properly analysed.
In the case of a conviction, who is liable, the manufacturer or the wholesale dealer ?
The man in whose possession the goods have been found and against whom conviction is secured. Any question between him and the manufacturer is a matter with which the department has nothing to do.

I would like again to refer to the question of the fertilizers in New Brunswick. Recently I had a conversation with a gentleman who resides in that province, and he informed me that it is a matter of very serious complaint in that province with the farmers that they are getting a very impure article, in fact, not at all what they ought to get for their money. I would like to know whether the department takes cognizance of this and whether analyses of fertilizers such as are there are made, and what the results are.

The chief analyst tells me that no complaint has been made to the department concerning fertilizers sold in New Brunswick. But if the hon. gentleman

(Mr. Henderson) can give us information on the subject I shall be glad to look into the question.
I will give the minister privately the name of my informant.
I have looked up the report of trade and commerce for 1904, and I find that pickles, sauces and catsups have been imported to the amount of no less than $371,000.
It is a pity that Canadians do not consume Canadian goods.

I quite agree with the minister, and I would go farther and say that it is a great pity that the government of this country does not put a duty upon these goods that would cause the Canadian goods to be consumed. But these adulterated goods are brought into the country and sold at such prices that our manufacturers cannot sell pure goods in competition with them, so, our manufacturers, to compete with this immense quantity of adulterated goods have to adulterate their own goods to a certain extent. The hon. member for York, N.B. (Mr. Crockett) has brought the matter of fertilizers before the House, and I am glad he has done it ? I do not believe that there is any commodity in which there is such a field for swindling the farmers as in fertilizers. The time has come when commercial fertilizers must b& used in this country. In the United States they are being used to an enormous extent. If there are any goods that ought to be analysed and in respect of which the people should be protected against fraud, they are commercial fertilizers.
Public .Works-chargeable to income-harbours and rivers-N. S., Apple river, wharf, $3,000.

I would like to say a word in a general way about these wharfs before we go on with the item. I find, in my own experience, a good many wharfs are built in places where they are absolutely useless. I should be glad if the minister would give some promise that all these wharfs that he is going to ask votes for to-night will be such as can be of use to those engaged in navigation and not merely to please individuals residing or having interests in the locality. I would draw the minister's attention to the fact that some peculiar expenditures are made out of votes given for wharfs. In the Auditor General's Report, with reference to the harbour improvements in Glace bay, it appears that some of the money voted was used to construct an earth railway embankment and trestle approach to the coal pier and to put down a sufficient number of railway tracks tbereon for the accommodation of traffic. I find that the Auditor General makes comment upon this expenditure as not being properly made in accordance with the vote. I think his ob-Mr. BRODEUR.
jection is well taken, it looks as if the expenditure was made in the interest of one corporation there'; and money voted for the construction of a wharf should hardly have been used for such a purpose. I know there is a wharf across the river in Hull, I suppose it cost $40,000 or $50,000, but I do not think the minister will say that that expenditure was justified by the amount of traffic done on that wharf. I hope he will assure the committee that he is not going to ask us to vote money to spend on wharfs that are going to be of so little use as that.

As regards the policy of the government in the erection of wharfs, I can assure the hon. geutleman that the department will take the greatest care in the expenditure of money. The circumstances under which wharfs are being constructed may be very different in one part of the country from those in another part. A wharf that might not be deemed necessary in the province of Quebec in a certain place where communication is largely by railway, might be necessary in another part of the country, on the great lakes or on the ocean, in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick, where there is no railway communication ; the expenditure might be justified in one case and not in another. In the particular case to which the hon. gentleman refers, I suppose, the Dominion Coal Company wanted to erect a wharf, and a wharf was also desired in the public interest. Therefore we made a business arrangement with the coal company, they erecting the wharf and we paying a certain amount of the cost. In that case we made provision towards building a wharf, because we knew that the public interest would be served by it. The company got what they want and the public are getting what they want from the construction of this wharf.

The explanation of the minister in that particular case seems to be satisfactory. I believe that the present acting minister has every intention of confining these expenditures to public purposes. I would like to ask him if the government has any policy with regard to the building of these wharfs, where to place them, and how much to expend upon them? I notice that last year there was a wharf built at a place called Lake Nominingue, in the province of Quebec. Now that is an inland lake somewhere about a hundred miles from the Ottawa river. There is nothing there I know of that the Department of Public Works has anything to do with. That is one reason why I ask if the government has any settled policy in building wharfs. I can understand the building of a wharf on the Ottawa river, which is a boundary between two provinces,, but I cannot understand why the Department of Public Works should build a wharf at this little lake called Nominingue, in a little place away back in the bush. It is the terminus of a railway, it is true, but at the

173a
same time it is an entirely provincial matter.
What is the cost of that wharf ? Have you got it there ?
$2,000 or $3,000. I am asking what the Dominion government has to do with building a wharf of that kind in the back woods ?

The hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken if he thinks we should only build wharfs on boundaries between provinces, or on the great lakes. It is the duty of the Public Works Department to build wharfs wherever they are required. That has been the policy of the Dominion government for many years. The hon. gentleman will understand that we cannot lay down any hard and fast rule with regard to these matters. As I have already tried to explain, a policy that might fit one province would not fit another. Those of us who are living where railway communication is easy must not forget that there are other places where there is no communication at all except by water. It is the duty of the government to take all these matters into consideration. We cannot lay down a hard and fast policy, I do not think the hon. gentleman himself could suggest any policy that would be better than to make expenditures wherever they are required in the public interest. We must consider every case on its merits, inquire into the character of the work, the cost of the work, and try to meet the needs of the people so far as' we can according to the funds at our disposal.

I believe the hon. minister said that wharfs are built wherever they are needed. I can tell him that he is very much mistaken. Would he tell me what is going to be done with regard to the pier at a place called Disraeli, in the county of Wolfe, for which $5,000 was voted last year ? Does the minister know anything about that pier, or does he care to know ? If he wants to know the history of that pier I will be glad to tell him.
Go on.

At that place there is a small stream flowing into a river. There is a dam below the mouth of the stream, and when the gates are shut the water rises in the dam and overflows into the creek, which is called Black creek. The people built a bridge over that creek some fifteen years ago. Last year the member for the county of Wolfe, I suppose it was that hon. gentleman, began to move in the matter. I must say that I honour that hon. gentleman's spunk. He got this government to vote $5,000 to build a pier, and that pier, I suppose, was intended to accommodate a steamboat. Now, Sir, where is the boat ?
I give it up.

There is no use for a boat, and there is no water to float a boat. I can tell the minister what was done. The people who live there are joking over this matter. The municipality gave a contract to parties to fill up this creek from one bank to the other, about 600 feet, with stone and earth, in order to make a roadway. Now that is the way that certain individuals blindfold the government. It is perfectly right; if I could blindfold the government myself I would do it, because municipalities have as much right to get help from the government as railway or steamboat companies have. I asked for a bridge once and I was refused. If you ask for $5,000 to build a bridge they will not listen to you. But, the hon. gentleman .lust pulls the wool over the government's eyes, asks for a vote and it is given to him. If the hon. minister will send his engineer there he would be able to ascertain what the conditions are. I suppose the money will not be paid until the work is done. If he sends his engineer there to oversee the work he will find nothing but a pile of stones. That is only a sample of it.
I may say that the items under discussion now are wharfs in Nova Scotia. I have no objection, of course
I do not blame you.

I have no objection, of course, to the discussion wandering far afield from the subject before the chair. As to the particular subject brought up by the hon. gentleman, I have no notes. Wharfs in Quebec will be reached in due time, and 1 would be very glad to give whatever explanation is possible in regard to the awful state of affairs the hon. gentleman has been depicting.

In view of the fact that the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) is absent, and as he is familiar with the Nova Scotia items, I would suggest to the hon. Minister of Public Works that we take up the Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick items, because, by doing so, we will make better headway than if we attempt to continue the consideration of the Nova Scotia items.
Why ?

For the simple reason that hon. members on this side of the House are not well acquainted witli the requirements of Nova Scotia. Unfortunately, our friends on the other side of the House have assisted in preventing us from getting our friends from that province to assist us in the discussion of these items.
When does the hon. gentleman expect to get any of his friends from Nova Scotia to help him to discuss these items ?
We are prepared to discuss the Prince Edward Island items.

If hon. gentlemen opposite will allow these items to pass, I will be very glad to allow one item to stand, on which any discussion can take place. The Department of Public Works have a large number of estimates to pass. I am sure I have tried to meet the convenience of hon. gentlemen opposite as far as possible in putting through items. If they will allow these items to go through, we will allow one item to stand on which any discussion can take place, and then we will take up the votes from Prince Edward Island.
The hon. gentleman might take up the Prince Edward Island items now, because the Prince Edward Island members are all here.

I know several hon. members on this side of the House who stayed here at great personal inconvenience just for the purpose of being here when these estimates are under consideration. I notified them this afternoon at three o'clock, asking them to stay, and now that they are here, I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite will not press the request which they have made.

Do we understand hon. members from Nova Scotia are going to take part in the discussion of these items ? I have no recollection of anything of that kind ever having occurred in the House. I think it is really unreasonable to expect the opposition to take these items up in view of the absence of the hon. leader of the opposition, who is the only man who understands the requirements of Nova Scotia.

It is a piece of nonsense for me to attempt to pass these items if hon. gentlemen opposite persist in their objection. If they say that they do not want the items to pass, it is impossible for me to go on with my estimates.
Has the hon. gentleman under his hand the information in regard to Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick ?
Yes.
In that case, I think we would make better headway by proceeding to the consideration of these items.

There is no doubt of it. We will not make any headway at all if hon. gentlemen opposite simply say that they will not go on with these estimates. I think, considering the number of estimates the department has to put through and the very fair offer I have made, that we should leave one item on which all the items may be discussed, hon. gentlemen might consent to the passing of these items.
We do not know any item to hold them up on.
Hold them up on any item you like, and discuss any of them afterwards.

The hon. minister tells us that they have no policy whatever in so far as wharfs in Nova Scotia are concerned. They have built them here, there and everywhere, and they do not intend to gite us any information in regard to them. We are unfamiliar with these estimates, but the hon. gentleman wants to run them through. We have our forces here from Prinee Edward Island, and we are prepared to go on with the Prince Edward Island items, and intelligently vote on them if a vote is required. We cannot hold ourselves down to one item, because we might pass the item in regard to which we require an explanation. Surely the hon. gentleman must have some policy in regard to wharfs in Nova Scotia, if they are to be anything more than local works or works of general advantage to the whole Dominion.

My hon. friend (Mr. Barr) hardly understands the suggestion of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works did not mean that the reservation of one item should confine the discussion to that one item. All these items are embraced in one resolution, and if you allow one item to stand, then the resolution as a whole will stand, and when subsequently he moved that the last item be carried the whole of these items will be open for discussion. That is what he proposes, so that my hon. friend does not have to pick out any one of them. He will be able to discuss any one of these items.
We are just where we were. Here is item 131, which we ask to be allowed to stand, but that request has been refused.

It seems to me that the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) is a fair and reasonable one. I cannot see that the suggestion of the hon. Minister of Public Works, as emphasized by the hon. Postmaster General, does the government a bit of good. It is not the same thing to have a discussion on one item when it goes through at some future day, because in five or ten minutes the whole thing is over. The only hon. gentleman on this side who has any knowledge of Nova Scotia is the hon. leader of the opposition, who is absent tonight. It is well known why he is absent, and I do not think it is right or fair for the government to pass these items in regard to Nova Scotia. The hon. leader of the opposition has bad an affliction in his family which the government must know of, and which has taken him away. He would be here except for that, and he is the only hon. gentleman on this side of the House who has any intimate knowledge of affairs in Nova Scotia. There is plenty of work for

this committee to do during the short time that we ought to continue to-night. We do not wish to be a party to obstructing the estimates of the bon. Minister of Public Works. We want to do this thing in a friendly way suitable to the convenience of hon. members, but the hon. leader of the opposition, being away, and the occasion of his being away being what it is, as is well known to the House, I think the hon. Minister of Public Works ought to comply with the request of my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram), who is the whip in charge of the opposition to-night in the House, and who, I think, is making a very reasonable proposition. We ought not to attempt to deal with any of the items in this resolution, but we should go on to the estimates for New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.

I do not wish to appear discourteous in any way, I am satisfied that we should go on with the New Bruns wick and Prince Edward Island items, but I feel, at the same time, that I have been really discourteous to hon. members on this side. The hon. member for East Elgin says that he has never heard the members on this side speak on these items. I am sure that the minister when putting through items should have the members for the constituencies with him to answer questions regarding the locality, the necessity for the work, &c. I do not see anything improper m that in any way ; it is the members' duty.
If I have hurt the hon. gentleman's feelings, I am very sorry.
My feelings are hurt-proof.
I must protest against this proceeding in the House. There are 18 members from Nova Scotia.
All on one side.

That is your fault, not ours. There are 17 members from Nova Scotia in the House I belieye, to-night. I know that three or four of them intended leaving to-day for their homes, but they were kept here tonight because these items were coming up. We are not like the Ontario and Quebec members who can go home every week end; we are kept here from the opening to the end of the session. My hon. friend from Elgin is not serious in saying that a member supporting the government should not be here. Take for instance the very first item that for Apple river. Apple river happens to be in my constituency and the hon leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) does not know any more about Apple river than does the hon. member for East Elgin.
Oh, yes he does.

He has never been within 50 miles of Apple river.

Is it fair and reasonable that simply because the leader of the opposition is not here
My hon. friend does not say that he should be here.

Higgin s shore pier-works of reconstruction and repairs, $1,000.
Will the hon. gentleman explain ?
Would the minister explain ?
It is a revote. Ordinary repairs to the existing wharf.
What work has to be done ?

This work is purely departmental work that the officers of the department recommended as being necessary. There is a crihwork revetment 120 feet by 12 feet wide and 6 feet high. There is an extension of the breakwater outward past a shoal, represented to be necessary to make the harbour safe of approach.
Will it be done by tender or by day work ?
The chances are by day work.
Is it the policy of the department in all repairs to breakwaters and wharfs and buildings to proceed by day work instead of by tender ?

The hon. gentleman will understand that there is great difficulty in small works of this kind in getting any one to tender, the difficulty being that the repairs that are necessary cannot be ascertained until probably some of the planks are removed. Within the last few days I had a case of calling for tenders for a work of this kind for a large amount, and it was impossible to have tenders because we could not give specifications; it simply said ' for renewal and contractors either refused to -tender or made their tenders upon the basis of an entirely new work. The policy is the same as that which has always been carried out by the Department of Public Works in works of this character.
Will this sum put it in good repair ?

That is the report of the officers of the department.

That is by tender ; it is under contract at the present time. This is to complete.

This is a very important wharf on the north side where harbours are not very numerous and where they are hard to approach. The fact that the item is in the estimates is proof that the government intends to go on with the work, but the cost is larger than we anticipated, and I am obtaining further information before asking parliament to supplement the vote.

The engineers of the government have been down there on more than one occasion, especially before the last elections, and the department ought now to have all the information it requires regarding the character of the work. I do not see the use of putting in a vote of $5,000, as was done last year and is now being done, and then telling the House that the department are waiting for the engineer's report, when the engineers have been down there and made their examination and ought to have reported. Surely if this wharf 1 cannot be built for $5,000 and the govern-

meut intend building it, they should ask a Richmond Bay, P.E.I.

Is it the intention of the department to go on with the work ?

If it be found to cost $30,000, I shall have to seriously consider whether I should ask for more money or let it wait. I hope we will be able to do the work for $15,000, but the estimates of the engineers are not entirely satisfactory, and I want to be certain before proceeding.
Repairs to piers and breakwaters, P.E.I., $6,-
000.

There are several works on the island which require immediate attention. One is the harbour at Mount Stewart in which I know the hon. gentleman from King's county (Mr. J. J. Hughes) is interested. That harbour requires dredging and also a little more wharf accommodation. The village is a growing one and has quite a large trade. If the minister can see his way clear to putting that harbour in repair, he will be doing a very necessary work.

I shall ask my engineer to take a note of the hon. gentleman's representations. My hon. friend will understand that this is not a vote for dredging but simply for repairs. Has the wharf he refers to been transferred to the government ?
I believe it has.
If not transferred to the government, we do not repair it.
Would it not. be in the same position as some wharfs you are building in Nova Scotia ?
When we build any wharfs in Nova Scotia, the title is with the government.

This is in the same position.

This is to enable the department to buy a certain amount of creosoted timber, so that we will be in a position to make repairs quickly.

No.
Has any action been taken for the purchase of the material ?

This is for the work of reconstruction and repairing.
Rustico harbour, P.E.I.-breakwater on Robinson's Island, south side of entrance to harbour, $11,000.

I understand that last fall a vessel went ashore there by reason of the channel having filled up with sand. Investigation was made by the government engineers to ascertain the cause, and the hon. minister will no doubt have some information on that point. If the filling in was caused by the construction of this breakwater, the breakwater may not have been put in the right place. Last fall a vessel went ashore there and the loss was attributed to the channel shifting. I understand an investigation took place, and that perhaps the minister has information which would enable him to state whether the disaster arose through the construction of this work, or in what other way.

We have no information in the department as to the cause of Ithe accident. I understand that this is a very difficult harbour. The object of this work is to produce, by the process of scouring, a channel which will always remain. The work is undertaken on the rep.ort of the engineer of the department which favours this as the proper way to carry it out.
There would appear to be two entrances to this harbour as there are two items.
There are two breakwaters, one on the north side and one on the south.
There is an item here of money paid to the King's Printer and charged to this work. What is that for ?
For printing the specifications.

Rustico harbour is one of the most important harbours on the north side. I see that this money was voted last year. I placed a question on the order paper as regards dredging done in Rustico harbour, and the minister, in reply, stated that there was none.
That is right.

I visited the place several times, and there was some dredging being done, but not by the usual dredge. Whether the Minister of Public Works has any knowledge of it or not, there was dredging there. Rustico harbour is in one of the most thickly settled parts of Prince Edward Island, and the people have been there a long time, many of them being French Aca-dians. There are many fishermen among them, yet they have no harbour or wharf accommodation. Their toil is very severe,

and some facilities for the pursuit of their avocation should be provided. For the last four or five years work has been done by day labour, and so badly done that the first storm swept it away. I hope that this time not only will a contract be given, but that the work will be promptly advertised and that there will be no delay.
Mr. LEFURGEY'. I would like to go back for a moment to Richmond bay, reconstruction of wharf, and ask the minister if he proposes to let that contract by tender ?

I think the present intention is to do it by day's work. I see in the memorandum before me all the items with estimate of cost. I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) heard me say that we advertised for tenders, but had no satisfactory response.
St. Peter's Bay-breakwater on east side of entrance to harbour, $7,500.
We would like some explanation about this ?

Tenders were called for, and some were received, but none of them satisfactory. Some ten days or two weeks ago, the resident engineer was asked to submit new plans and specifications, and on these, tenders will be called for.
I am a new member of the House and not thoroughly posted in the rules, but I think there is not a quorum present.

I think the hon. member (Mr. Lalor) will find that there is a quorum ; twenty make a quorum and there are more than twenty members present.
Summerside harbour-breakwater, $20,000.
In what year was this work first before the House ?

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) has had a number of opportunities of discussing it. I think it was in 1899 that the matter was first brought before the House. The contract for the work was let in 1900.
I think it first came up in 1898.
I am only judging by the date of the contract.
Were tenders received for the work in 1898 ?
What was the cause of the delay for those two years ?

I have heard the hon gentleman discuss this subject several times. But, I shall be glad to go over it again. The hon. gentleman knows the situation there. There was a great question as to the charac-Mr. A. MARTIN.
ter of the work to be constructed in that harbour. It is a very long breakwater- 2,300 or 2,400 feet, if I am not mistaken-and a difficult work. After a certain progress had been made on the contract, the engineer of the department reported that it was questionable whether the character of the work being done in the shallower portion would be suitable for the whole work, and the contract, therefore, was not gone on with. A settlement was made with the contractor and the work has remained in that position ever since. So far as the department is concerned, I asked not only the engineer of the department, but the deputy to visit the work to see how it was standing the ravages of the ocean. The hon. gentleman knows that this is a very exposed place, and he knows that such a work as this has to be carefully considered. I have not fully persuaded myself that it would be in the interest of the public, or of the people of Summerside to make the rest of the work of the same character as that already done. I had hoped to \isit Summerside last year, but was unable to do so. I have engineers making a full report as to the matter, whether we dare continue that work in the way it has been begun. There are few works of this character, and I am sure the hon. members from Prince Edward Island would not like to see a work gone on with that would be in danger of early destruction by the sea.

From the minister's standpoint what he has said may seem a plausible excuse for not finding out in the first place whether the work, as designed, would fulfil the purpose for which it was intended. It seems to me that the time from 1898 or 1897, when the plans were prepared and the matter brought before this House up to this year, is ample for the department to make up its mind. Now, in 1897 or 1898 when this work was called for, the department must have investigated and found that there was a necessity for it. The department must have reasonably satisfied themselves through their experts that the work would accomplish a great benefit to the harbour of Summerside. They must also have found out the class of work that would be required, and the conditions to which this breakwater would be subject to. They must have found out before asking for tenders that the work would be reasonably suitable to withstand the sea, and frost, and so forth. It seems to me that the department, after calling for tenders and getting a tender for $54,000, have been very lax in the pursuance of their duties in not pressing this tenderer to continue the work, or take it out of his hands and have an investigation in a year or two after the contractor had failed to proceed with this work. Now, we find that the contract was let in 1900, and here we are in 1905, and the minister comes and explains that he has sent a man down three or four years after the work has been

stopped to find out if the work is corroding, if it is standing the weather and the sea.
The hon. gentleman says three or four years, as a matter of fact he went down in March, 1904.
If the minister will look up the ' Hansard ' he will find that we have been questioning the minister in respect to this Summerside breakwater ever since 1900. There was no work going on in 1904.
We stopped the work in 1904.

In 1900, when I was running an election In the county of East Prince, there was a flaring poster, as I have already told the House, published broadcast through the streets of Summer-side, announcing that a breakwater would be built, and that from $15,000 to $20,000 per month would be spent on this work, and what a great boon it would be to the workingmen of Summerside. This work has been promised for years and years, and no further progress has been made. If it is the policy of this government to revote a work three or four years in succession to find out whether the class of work recommended by the department will stand the weather, then the public works of this country will be in a very bad state before we get anything accomplished. Now, I find that votes have been passed every year since 1898. I believe we figured it up a year or two ago and found that the votes and revotes for a contract that was originally to cost $54,000, amounted to $108,000 in the session of 1903. I think we had a vote last year and now we find another vote this year ; so that altogether for a work that was originally to cost $54,000, we have voted over $150,000. All this time we find our Liberal friends in that province pointing to this aggregate of votes and saying : See how great an amount of money we are getting for public works in Prince Edward Island. I want to point out how the people of Prince Edward Island are being fooled in the matter of public works. In the estimates of last year there was a paltry sum of $13,000 for public works in Prince county, and I find that this year, of that $13,000, $10,400 is a revote- only $2,600 has been spent in the county of Prince during the last year. I am not objecting to the minister's estimates with regard to the amount of money voted for public works in the county I have the honour to represent. But I must insist upon the department proceeding with some degree of speed on the public works which are admitted by them to be required for the benefit of the shipping of that county. 1 would like to know from the minister whether they intend to build this work, if a new plan has been put before the government, and whether they will call for tenders for this work in the near future. I have received by the last mail letters from people in Summerside asking whether this work is to be continued.

I should be very sorry to remove anything from the estimates which would deprive the hon. gentleman of an opportunity of getting off the speech he has made on several occasions. The work is exactly in the position I have told him.
I cannot alter the conditions. If it is found that a work can be constructed there of a character that will stand and serve the purpose, that breakwater will be constructed. The engineer has been asked to report; and when we get his report the department will decide what to do.
Will the minister tell me how they propose to go on ?

By a new contract, by making plans and specifications for a work which will be of a character to ensure permanency. It is unfortunate, I acknowledge, the hon. gentleman has some grievance when he says that over $100,000 have been voted, and so little has been spent. He objects because a certain vote has been a re vote.
It is to blind the people.

I quite concede that the people of the county have been blinded. But let the hon. gentleman possess his soul in patience. We will have the work investigated. I have no desire to delay the work if it is necessary. This is a very long work, some 2,900 feet, and it is necessary that it should be made of a permanent character when it is undertaken.

I think the department should now be seized of the knowledge whether this breakwater is going to be built, and how it is going to be built. Surely the people of Summerside ought not to be obliged to wait another year for that breakwater. Will the minister assure me that plans and specifications will be prepared, and tenders called for, and the work proceeded with in the spring 1

There is no hon. gentleman to whom I would like better to give such an assurance. But I cannot give an assurance of that kind after the statements I have made that it is necessary for the department to be perfectly sure of the char-aster of the work which they contemplate constructing there, in order that it may be of a permanent character. The hon. gentleman knows as well as I do that there are great difficulties, it is a large undertaking. He knows that a breakwater of that length reaching out into deep water requires to be carefully considered. I can only give the hon. gentleman the assurance that I will have reports from the engineers, and when we are satisfied of the proper

character of the work to construct there, we will go on.
There is no doubt the minister will find that they can put a breakwater there that will fill the bill.
There is no doubt that we could put a breakwater there that would fill the bill, but it would possibly cost $200,000 or $300,000. The question of cost comes in.
Then it is a question of cost ?
Very largely.
May I ask the hon. minister what length they would go to in constructing a breakwater in Summerside harbour ?

The good faith of the de partment is shown in entering into the original contract in 1900. The amount of that contract was $55,000. I do not think that the extension of a work of that character all the way could be carried out for that money. It is a question of cost, and we want to be sure before we proceed with the work. If, having a vote for $20,000, I entered into a contract for a work that would cost $150,000 or $200,000, I would be very seriously critcised in this House.

I think the hon. gentleman said last year that the amount that would be required to complete that work satisfactory would be in the neighbourhood of $150,000. May I ask the hon. gentleman if, in case the department find that a useful work can be constructed for that amount of money, we can have his assurance that the work will go on after a careful investigation has been made ? I presume they have the details of this work in the department, and if he decides that it can be advantageously proceeded with at a cost of $150,000, will the hon. gentleman give us the assurance that it will be gone on with ?

I am sorry I cannot give the hon. gentleman that definite assurance. I do not think I would be justified, with a vote of $20,000, in entering into a contract for a work that would cost,$150,000.

Harbours and rivers. New Brunswick-Camp-bellton-wharf extension and repairs, $50,000.
Would the hon. gentleman give us a little explanation about that ?

This work is under contract. The contract was let on the 11th October, and amounted to $35,300. In addition to that, the department were called upon, as the result of an arbitration, to pay $35,000 for the wharf. It is only fair to tell the committee that from the information the department have it will be necessary to ask for another vote in the supplementary estimates. The wharf at Camp-bellton is not at all sufficient for the amount of business that is being done there. There is the boat service by the south shore, which it will be imperative practically to provide a landing for. In addition to that, the number of boats loading lumber every year and the shipping generally are increasing to such an extent that the department will be justified in asking the House for a further vote, on which this whole work can be discussed.
What will the total cost be ?
The amount of the contract which has been entered into is $35,300.

I know that Monday is private members' day. Perhaps the hon. minister can tell us, if private members get through with their business, what the government propose to do after that ?

'Mr. HYMAN. Private members' work will be taken up, and if we get through with that we will go into supply.
On what items ?
I cannot answer that, but it will not be on the Public Works estimates.
Could any of the ministers say what estimates they will discuss ?

It is a difficult matter. If the hon. Minister of Agriculture is here, I think he will go on with his estimates, but I would not like to be bound down to saying exactly what we will go on with. It will be private members' day, and I suppose it will be taken up with private members' business. -
